1.0:
Speak to the Israelites and say to them, ‘Should any person from you bring forward to YHWH an offering, of beasts from herd and from flock you shall bring forward your offering...
Rabbi Benamozegh begins his foray into Vayiqra with a contextual presentation of the origins and purpose of animal sacrifices. He addresses the misconceptions held by both ancient and contemporary scholars.
The heart of Rabbi Benamozegh’s argument lies in challenging the notion that the practice of sacrifices originated from human initiative rather than God’s command.
He first takes aim at his Italian counterpart Shadal, who held that sacrifices were adopted as a way for people to express gratitude, seek favour, or appease God, similar to how they might try to please a human king. It follows that the Torah, focusing more on guiding people towards righteousness than imparting knowledge, therefore did not abolish sacrifices. Shadal argues that sacrifices were neither inherently evil nor harmful but beneficial in cultivating certain values. He suggests that if the Torah had rejected sacrifices in favour of intangible practices like prayer or moral preaching, it would not have impressed the masses as much. People of that era, and generally in all times, tend to honour what appears grand and self-exalting. Therefore, to instil the fear and greatness of God in people’s hearts and deter them from erring, the concept of sacrifices was adopted by the Torah. This system served to constantly remind the people of the presence of a great God and King among them, fostering a sense of closeness and favour with God through these acts of service.
Rabbi Benamozegh disagrees with Shadal, and fundamentally so. In his view, Shadal’s approach aligns mistakenly with that of the heretic Baruch Spinoza, who he believes also undervalued the Torah’s intent to impart wisdom and knowledge. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this perspective dangerously limits the Torah to mere guidance in righteousness, ignoring its deeper educational purpose.
Rabbi Benamozegh extends this critique to the Christian interpretation of sacrifices, seeing a parallel in their effort to distance themselves from the Torah’s yoke. Christians, he notes, deemed many commandments as relevant only to the time in which they were given and not intrinsically valuable, a view shared by reformist Jews who favour only the Torah’s moral teachings. Especially in the view of some Christian theologians, the cultic laws, such as sacrifices, were viewed as primitive, and needed only by primitive people who could not reach salvation in the moral teachings of Jesus. According to Rabbi Benamozegh, the view of Shadal undermines the inherent sanctity and transformative power of the commandments, reducing them to mere arbitrary tools for instilling fear and love of God.
Rabbi Benamozegh addresses the connection between Shadal and the 12th century Spaniard, Rambam, who also acknowledged that sacrifices are not inherently desired by God, but rather serve a specific purpose: they were essential in weaning the Israelites from the idolatrous practice of child sacrifice and guiding them towards monotheism. According to Shadal and Rambam, the notion that God does not ‘desire’ the sacrifices would create confusion among the people, and so the Torah could not explicitly forbid them; if sacrifices are not desired, then people might question whether God truly desires anything from them, even righteousness!
Rabbi Benamozegh does not accept this line of reasoning, as he does not see how the cause (in this case, commanding sacrifices) leads to the effect (moving the people away from idolatry). He attempts to undermine the very core of Rambam’s argument that the Israelites would require a transitionary system (animal sacrifices) for a previously idolatrous practice (human sacrifices). After all, he notes that Moshe was very bold in abolishing deeply ingrained practices and prohibiting idolatry and images. He describes how Moshe initiated such drastic changes, moving the nation from one extreme to another, even prohibiting practices that did not seem inherently harmful but resembled those of the other nations. With this analysis, he is essentially asking Rambam the following: why couldn’t Moshe do the same for sacrifices? Ultimately, Rabbi Benamozegh contends that the continuity of such a significant tradition (sacrifices) could only be justified if it were inherently good and desirable in the eyes of God.
Rabbi Benamozegh then refers to the support that Rambam finds in Sefer Yirmiyahu for the position that the sacrificial system was not commanded by God because they were intrinsically commendable but rather to distance Israel from idolatry, “For when I freed your ancestors from the land of Egypt, I did not speak with them or command them concerning burnt offerings or sacrifice. But this is what I commanded them: Do My bidding, that I may be your God and you may be My people; walk only in the way that I enjoin upon you, that it may go well with you.” (7:22-23)
Rabbi Benamozegh critiques this interpretation, arguing that it falls short of proving its intended point. He notes that sacrifices were actually offered by Israelites in Egypt, and immediately after their exit. The Torah in fact commands that this offering – the Pesaḥ offering – be kept for all future generations. Thus, Rabbi Benamozegh suggests that just as one cannot interpret Yirmiyahu’s words in a way that denies an obvious commandment of Israel, that of sacrifices, one cannot conclude that there is no inherent purpose to those sacrifices.
Rabbi Benamozegh goes on to offer what he believes is the correct interpretation of the abovementioned verse in Yirmiyahu. He states that the verse was intended to correct misconceptions about the nature of sacrificial services, stressing the importance of accompanying moral and ethical conduct alongside ritual observance. Therefore, upon their departure from Egypt and their commitment to becoming a nation dedicated to the Lord and the observance of His commandments, God did not provide them with specific obligations regarding sacrifices (as the verse states, “I did not speak with them or command them concerning burnt offerings or sacrifice”). Instead, their commitment was a general acceptance to uphold the entire Torah, recognising its essential nature, where no individual commandment could absolve the obligation to fulfil another. Consequently, the following verse in Yirmiyahu states, “this is what I commanded them: Do My bidding, that I may be your God and you may be My people; walk only in the way that I enjoin upon you, that it may go well with you.” Rabbi Benamozegh argues that these verses are stating that there is no justification for prioritising physical sacrifices and rituals over moral conduct, virtues, and internalised worship. In this light, sacrifices, while essential, are not sufficient on their own; they must be part of a broader spiritual and ethical life to achieve their intended purpose.
Rabbi Benamozegh continues by noting that all he has done here is defend the commandment of sacrifices from attacks that it is not intrinsically valuable, and has attempted to show that it is. He directs the reader to the renowned Sefer Kuzari by the 11th century Spaniard Rabbi Yehuda Halevy, which agrees with his position that sacrifices are inherently meaningful, and in fact lists them above the level of so-called ‘moral’ laws, which relate to justice and righteousness, and form a more basic set of laws.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh concludes by discussing one further proof brought by those in the opposing camp, which is to be found in Aḥare Mot. A verse there states that the Israelites in the desert are not to slaughter animals wherever they like, outside of the tabernacle. They are only to be allowed to slaughter in the tabernacle, as an offering. This is used by some to show that the Israelites needed to be weaned away from sacrificing to whichever gods they chose as and when they liked, and that this was achieved by centralising the cultic worship. From this, the parallel to the general commandment of sacrifices is drawn. Rabbi Benamozegh rejects this suggestion, stating that the real prohibition here is not on idolatry but on indulging in meat to satiate their physical drives. The reason that this is forbidden is indeed because the Israelites at that time were susceptible to the idolatrous influences of the nations around them, who would sacrifice to their gods anywhere, but this is secondary to the prohibition itself, which is against meat consumed for physical pleasure. He supports this conclusion by pointing out that this prohibition was only for the Israelites in the desert, and did not last eternally, as the command for sacrifices does.

4.0:
And he shall slaughter the male of the herd before YHWH, and the sons of Aharon, the priests, shall bring forward the blood and cast the blood round the altar which is at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
Rabbi Benamozegh focuses on the act of slaughtering as described in the verse.
He points out that according to the Jewish tradition passed down by our ancestors, the task of slaughtering was not exclusively reserved for priests. In this context, he highlights that laymen, or non-priestly individuals, were also considered competent to perform this sacred act.
He further substantiates this claim by referring to the testimony of the 1st century BCE Jewish scholar, Philo of Alexandria. Although Philo was not thoroughly versed in the teachings of Ḥazal, he corroborated the veracity of this tradition in his own works, in which he notes that during the time of the Passover sacrifice, there was no distinction made between priests and Israelites in performing the slaughter.

10.0:
And he shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before YHWH, and the sons of Aharon, the priests, shall cast its blood round the altar.
Rabbi Benamozegh begins by acknowledging the richness of Kabbalistic interpretations associated with sacrifices, suggesting that a full exploration of these would reveal the act of sacrifice as a deeply righteous one, firmly rooted in the depth of the Written Torah.
A notable point in his commentary is the emphasis on the geographical orientation of the sacrifices – specifically, that sacrifices for transgressions are slaughtered in the north. He argues that this is not a mere directional choice; it holds deep symbolic significance. The north, in Kabbalistic thought, represents the force of strict justice and judgement. This is particularly fitting for transgressors, who are encouraged to direct their penitence towards this symbolic point of Divine judgement. Their physical act of bowing and prostrating in this direction reflects their spiritual contrition and acknowledgment of their misdeeds.
Rabbi Benamozegh further draws an intriguing comparison between the sacrifices and the garments of the High Priest, which are made of mixed fabrics. This comparison is rooted in the Kabbalistic understanding of the universe. The prohibition against wearing mixed fabrics (sha’atnez) is based on the idea of keeping distinct and opposing forces separate. However, in the context of the Holy Temple, where sacrifices are offered, these opposing forces are deliberately brought together. The sacrifices, performed according to specific measures and principles, symbolise the unification of these opposing elements. In this sacred space, the mixing of different kinds – which is normally forbidden – becomes not just permissible but a commandment. Rabbi Benamozegh notes that this is a manifestation of the ultimate unity and harmony that the Temple embodies.

1.0:
And he shall bring it to the sons of Aharon, the priests, and a handful from there shall be scooped up, from its fine semolina and from its oil, together with all its frankincense, and the priest shall turn its token portion to smoke on the altar, a fire offering, a fragrant odour to YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh provides an explanation for the act of pinching during sacrificial offerings.
He references a tradition among Ḥazal that specifies the use of the fourth finger for the pinching of the handful required in this verse, known as ‘qemiṣa’. He states that the use of this finger is linked to ancient practices, as he cites the work of Macrobius, an authority on ancient customs, in Book VII of his Saturnalia.
Macrobius writes that Horus observed Egyptian priests, referred to as ‘prophets’, performing rituals in their temples. These priests anointed the fourth finger of the left hand of the statues of their gods with precious perfumes. When Horus asked the priests why they chose that finger, they answered that this specific finger, when folded, symbolises the number six - a number that was considered divine and is a perfect number (meaning that it is the sum of its divisors).
Rabbi Benamozegh highlights two notable points in this context. Firstly, he contrasts the practice of the Egyptian priests, who anointed the left hand, with the Israelite custom of using the right hand, a key difference in ritualistic approaches. Secondly, he acknowledges that while the reason for choosing this particular finger is not explicitly mentioned in the writings of Ḥazal, the wisdom found in Gentile traditions, as reported by Macrobius, bears the seal of Kabbalistic wisdom, lending a universal aspect to this ritualistic practice.
Furthermore, Rabbi Benamozegh encourages exploration of the anatomical and symbolic importance of this finger in broader contexts, such as human dissection and composition. He references a popular work of his era, Les Mystères de la Main by Desbarrolles, a chiromancer, that delved into the mysteries and significance of the hand, and this finger in particular, suggesting a deeper, perhaps even esoteric, understanding of human anatomy.

10.0:
Any grain offering that you bring forward to YHWH shall not be made leavened, for you shall not turn to smoke any leaven nor any honey from it as a fire offering to YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the significance of the prohibition of leaven and honey in offerings as mentioned in the verse.
He notes that in ancient times, various nations had a practice where honey was specifically offered to the gods they believed ruled the underworld (the mythical home of the dead, imagined as being under the earth). This choice was rooted in their cultural and religious beliefs, where offering honey to the gods of the heavens, rather than the gods of the underworld, was considered a profound abomination.
Rabbi Benamozegh’s analysis indicates a parallel between these ancient practices and the teachings of the Torah. The Torah’s instruction to refrain from using honey in offerings aligns with the idea that such offerings were not suitable for the God of Israel. Rabbi Benamozegh supports this correlation with references from the work of the 2nd century Roman philosopher, Porphyry of Tyre, where similar themes and practices are discussed.

12.0:
And if all the community of Israel should err, and the thing be hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do one of all YHWH’s commands that should not be done, and they bear guilt...
Rabbi Benamozegh, citing the wisdom of Ḥazal, states that “all the community” (כל עדת) refers to the Sanhedrin, the supreme council and tribunal of elders and officers leading the nation of Israel.
He argues against later commentators who disagreed with this interpretation, presenting two main reasons to substantiate his view.
Firstly, Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises the representative role of the elders and officers. Just as an emissary embodies the one who sent him, so do these leaders represent the entire populace of Israel. Therefore, when they are involved in a matter, it is as if the entire nation is involved, warranting the term “all the community”.
Secondly, he draws attention to Scriptural nuances that distinguish “all the community” from “Israel”. For example, in Bemidbar 25:6, it is stated that both “Israel” and “all the community” are present, indicating they are not the same entity.
Further, in Bemidbar 35:24, the term “all the community” is used exclusively for the Sanhedrin in the context of judgement. This distinction is reiterated in the story of Pineḥas, where “all the community” cannot mean the entire assembly of Israel but rather the elders, given the spatial and situational context.
In a similar way, Rabbi Benamozegh points to the term עם meaning ‘people’, which can also stand as a synecdoche (a rhetorical device where a part is used to represent the whole or the whole for a part) for the chiefs of the people. He evidences this from the statement attributed to the עם in Yitro, but which in Va’etḥanan is attributed to the heads of the people.

21.0:
When a prince offends and does one of all the commands of YHWH his God that should not be done, in error, and he bears guilt...
Rabbi Benamozegh begins by identifying the “prince” or “chieftain” (נשיא) mentioned in the verse as ‘the king’, drawing on the interpretations of the 18th century German Hebraist, Rabbi Naftali Wessely.
Delving into historical context, Rabbi Benamozegh explains that in many nations, including among the Israelites before the establishment of the Davidic monarchy, the king was essentially the foremost among princes and judges. This perspective views the king not as a distinct entity but as an elevated prince (נשיא). He supports this by noting that even after the cessation of the traditional kingdom in Israel, the role of the ‘nasi’ persisted, guiding the assembly’s head. This historical continuity underscores the enduring importance of the ‘nasi’ in Jewish leadership.
He supports this with an example from the kingdom of Aragon, where the king’s authority was contingent on his adherence to established norms and expectations, as recorded by the 18th century French philosopher Nicolas Antoine Boulanger. This example further illustrates the shared authority and mutual obligations between a king and his subjects in historical governance systems.
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses a misunderstanding about the phrase מלך רבי (‘a certain rabbi ruled’), which appears in the Talmud such as in Ta’anit 21a. He clarifies that it signifies a rabbi’s appointment as a ‘nasi’, which fits his description of the role of king. Thus, utilising this phrase was not an act of arrogance or false pride. He counters the notion that such titles were used boastfully, grounding his argument in historical and cultural comparisons. For instance, he cites a work by 18th century Italian philosopher Giambattista Vico, which details how early French monarchs were essentially ‘first among peers’. This comparison is used to illustrate how kings from the house of David functioned similarly - as the head of the Sanhedrin, with judicial responsibilities as the first among equals on that judicial body.
Further elaborating on the judicial role of kings, Rabbi Benamozegh references Scriptural mandates for justice and judgement, highlighting the unique position of Davidic kings in both judging and being judged. This dual role is seen as a continuation of the function of ‘nasi’, maintaining leadership over the Sanhedrin as long as they existed among the Israelites.

31.0:
And the right thigh you shall give as a levy to the priest from the communion sacrifices.
Rabbi Benamozegh continues to explore the various rituals associated with offering sacrifices, particularly focusing on the significance of the right thigh in various ancient cultures.
He notes that there was a custom among ancient cultures of burning the thigh of a sacrificial animal on an altar as an offering to their deity, rather than giving the thigh to the priests. This ritual was prevalent among the Greeks, as he illustrates with the example of Hercules offering a sacrifice to Zeus in Olympia, a story documented by the 2nd century CE geographer Pausanias in Book V of his famous work, Description of Greece.
Further expanding on this theme, Rabbi Benamozegh refers to a work by the 17th century French historian Antoine Banier, which asserts that such customs of offering sacrifices were widespread among different nations. However, he also mentions the dissertation of 19th century Italian jurist, Giuseppe De Cesare, which provides a contrasting view. De Cesare wrote that there were nations that burnt only the innards of the animal upon the altar, but did not burn the other parts, such as the thigh.
Rabbi Benamozegh then makes a significant theological connection between these ancient practices and Israelite rituals. He points out that in these ancient cultures, what was consecrated for the altar and offered to the deities, namely the thigh of the sacrifice, was designated in Israelite tradition to be consumed by the priests.
He further contextualises this by examining the Israelite dietary evolution during their time in the desert. During this period, the Israelites were in a transitional state, not yet fully adherent to the later, albeit temporary, prohibitions against consuming ‘meat of desire’ - meat not offered as a sacrifice. This was a time when Israelite dietary practices were shifting from the broader Noaḥide laws to more distinct, Israelite-specific regulations. In this phase, the consumption of meat by the Israelites was still predominantly through sacrificial offerings.
His analysis of this point continues, as he observes that the offerings made by Gentiles (as exemplified by Noaḥ) consist of animals that are fit for Jews to eat. Thus, the animals on the ‘high level’ of pagan sacrifices are lowered to the public consumption of the Jewish people. This is in the same way as the thigh, which was wholly burnt on pagan alters, is ‘demoted’ to the consumption of the Jewish priests. Rabbi Benamozegh sees this as emphasising the role of the Jewish people as priests to the entirety of humanity.

23.0:
And he brought forward the sons of Aharon, and Moshe put from the blood on their right earlobe and on the thumb of their right hand and on the big toe of their right foot, and Moshe cast the blood on the altar all around.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the significance of the anointing of certain body parts during the consecration of priests, offering insights into the symbolism behind these rituals.
He starts by examining the anointing of the earlobe, suggesting it symbolises liberation from physical labour and servitude. This contrasts with the practice of piercing a servant’s ear, signifying perpetual servitude, a custom also observed in ancient Greece.
He then turns to the anointing of the right thumb, highlighting its significance in consecrating the priests’ hands, their primary tool for performing sacred services. He emphasises the thumb’s crucial role in the hand, without which the other fingers would be ineffective. He contrasts the anointing of the thumb to the practice of Adoni-Bezeq in Sefer Shofetim, who cut off the thumbs and big toes of kings whom he had conquered. This point is also illustrated with a historical reference to the Athenians, who punished the rebellious by amputating their thumbs, thereby rendering their hands useless.
The commentary then addresses the anointing of the big toe, interpreted as a way to sanctify the priests’ movements towards the Holy Temple. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this act ensures their walk is peaceful and purposeful. He notes that the Tanakh often uses foot and walking metaphors to represent the integrity, or the lack thereof, in actions.
Rabbi Benamozegh thus concludes his explanation for the selection of these specific organs for anointing. However, he admits uncertainty about why the right side was chosen over the left side, other than the general sacredness attributed to the right side in Jewish tradition. He concludes by drawing a parallel between the wisdom of Ḥazal and the teachings of the Torah about giving precedence to the right side over the left, suggesting they are inherently connected and bear the same mark of Divine truth.

32.0:
And from the entrance of the Tent of Meeting you shall not go out seven days, until the day of completion of the days of your installation, for seven days shall your initiation be.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the concept of “filling of hands” (ימלא את ידכם) which connotes a form of ‘consecration’, ‘ordination’, or ‘initiation’.
He critiques the explanation given by Rabbi Naftali Wessely, an 18th century German Hebraist, who posited that the “filling of hands” means to imbue a person with strength, in opposition to the phrases ‘lack of hand’ or ‘short-hand’, both idioms for weakness. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this interpretation does not fully capture the essence of the phrase. He suggests that ‘strength of hand’ would be a more appropriate contrast to ‘lack of hand’ rather than “filling of hand”.
Rabbi Benamozegh then presents his understanding of the phrase, connecting it to the initiation or installation into a sacred service. He explains that before initiation, a person’s hands are metaphorically empty. It is only when one starts serving and engaging with the holy vessels or sacrifices that their hands are considered ‘full’. This filling of the hands (ימלא את ידכם) symbolises an ordination or initiation, the moment one’s hands transition from emptiness to being filled with sacred tasks.
He supports his interpretation with other verses that state how Aharon and his sons began their service by physically handling sacred objects and performing rituals as commanded by God, as recorded in Vayiqra 8:27, “[Moshe] put everything on the palms of Aharon and on the palms of his sons, and elevated them as an elevation offering before YHWH.”

2.0:
And Moshe said to Aharon, “This is just what YHWH spoke, saying, ‘Through those close to Me shall I be hallowed and in all the people’s presence shall I be honoured.’”
Rabbi Benamozegh uses this verse to analyse the relationship between the Written Torah and the Oral Law.
He starts by noting an apparent discrepancy in our verse: it states, “this is what YHWH meant by saying”, but there is no record in the Torah of God saying these words to Moshe. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this implies not everything God told Moshe was written down in the Torah - many commands and teachings were given orally.
Rabbi Benamozegh engages in a detailed critique of 19th century Italian scholar Shadal, who tried to reconcile this discrepancy by comparing this verse to a narrative involving Laban, Bethuel, and Eliezer in Sefer Bereshit. This narrative, found in Bereshit 24, describes Eliezer’s journey to find a wife for Yiṣḥaq, where he encounters Ribka and witnesses events that he interprets as Divine signs. Shadal suggests that the phrase “this is what YHWH meant by saying” in our verse is akin to the Divine intervention in Eliezer’s story, where Laban and Bethuel recognise God’s hand in the events, even though His involvement in that story is not explicitly written.
Rabbi Benamozegh identifies two key errors in this comparison. First, he argues that Shadal’s interpretation is unnecessary because the Divine guidance in Eliezer’s encounter with Ribka is already clear and direct in the narrative, without the need for further allegorical interpretation. Second, he challenges the application of this interpretation to our verse, where the phrase “this is what YHWH meant by saying” appears to indicate a direct, explicit command from God that was previously stated. In contrast, the guidance in Eliezer’s story is indirect, revealed through events rather than explicit Divine speech.
He then delves into the analysis of the plague of locusts in Sefer Shemot. In this narrative, the command of the plague is not explicitly detailed in the text. The 12th century French commentator Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor suggests that this omission of an explicit command from God is intentional, aimed at brevity, and that this is the same as our verse here. However, Rabbi Benamozegh strongly rejects this take too. He argues, granted the command for the plague of locusts need not be included, but why would such a statement as the one in our verse be left out simply to be concise? He considers the deaths of those closest to the service of God to be too essential a statement of God to be left out simply for the sake of brevity. Rabbi Benamozegh also asserts that given the explicit mention of Divine speech in the text (“this is what YHWH meant by saying”), it is more reasonable to assume that God did indeed speak those words to Moshe, even if those words were not recorded in the Torah.
2.1:
Rabbi Benamozegh then discusses the meaning of the end of the verse, that “Through those close to me I shall be hallowed.” He notes that the 11th century French commentator Rashi links these words to those in Shemot 29, where God says, “I shall be hallowed by my glory”, and that this is an example of the interconnectedness of the books of the Torah.
Lastly, Rabbi Benamozegh addresses the absence of detailed instructions for certain ritual practices, specifically the ritual sprinklings. He notes that Rashi observes this absence in his own commentary, implying that not every Divine command was explicitly written in the Torah. For if the command was not given at all, then the Israelites of the time would have challenged Moshe for the source of these ritual practises, in much the same way as contemporary deniers of the Oral Law challenge it and accuse the rabbis of fabricating it. Rabbi Benamozegh observes that Moshe received both the Written and Oral Laws, and while the Written Law was recorded, the Oral Law was not, and we cannot expect Moshe to live through each generation reassuring them that this tradition is authentic too, just as the tradition of the Written Law.

5.0:
And Moshe said to Aharon and to Eleazar and to Itamar his sons, “Your heads you shall not dishevel nor your garments rend, lest you die and the fury come upon the whole community...
Rabbi Benamozegh presents a multifaceted exploration of this verse based on historical context, particularly in relation to Egyptian traditions.
Our verse states, “your heads you shall not dishevel”, which Rabbi Benamozegh believes is further expanded in Yeḥezkel 44:20 as “They shall not shave their heads nor let their hair go untrimmed; they shall keep their hair trimmed.” He notes that the Sages interpret “trim” (כסם) in a specific way, where the hair is kept short enough that the top of each hair borders on the root of the next hair, but is not shaved completely. This haircut is attributed to Ben Elạsa, who is related by the Talmud to have spent a large amount of money to have his hair cut this way, in order to show what the haircut of the Kohen Gadol looked like.
This interpretation is supported by historical references to Egyptian priests who were described similarly. These priests had very short hair, cut in a circle that went round the back of the head, a detail documented in Book II of 17th century archaeologist and monk Bernard de Montfaucon’s ‘L’antiquité expliquée et représentée en figures,’ cited in the work of Masonic writer Reghellini de Scio.
Rabbi Benamozegh insists that the similarities between Israelite and Egyptian customs do not imply mere imitation. Instead, it suggests that the Egyptians, more than other nations, preserved significant elements of appropriate ideas and practices. This assertion is reinforced by elements of Kabbalistic teachings, which did not recognise the potential benefits and dangers inherent in this as a general principle.
A clear example of this principle is seen in the comparison of ancient laws between Israel and Egypt. Esteemed Roman historians like Tacitus and Suetonius observed the similarities in beliefs between Israelites and Egyptians, concluding that these beliefs were, in Rabbi Benamozegh’s words, “stamped with one seal”. However, Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises that Moshe’s approach to Egyptian beliefs and customs was not to simply imitate them, but only to do those practices which were correct, as evidenced in God’s warning in Vayiqra 18:3, “Like the practice of the land of Egypt in which you dwelt, you shall not do...”
Rabbi Benamozegh moves on to carefully contrast the paths taken by Israel and Greece, two nations who had been influenced by Egyptian culture. While Israel is described as having ascended, surpassing their Egyptian predecessors, the Greeks, despite deriving their beliefs and customs from the same source, are depicted as having descended, falling below even the Egyptians in terms of spiritual and cultural development.
5.1: Additionally, Rabbi Benamozegh touches on how Egypt is perceived in Kabbalistic thought. To the Kabbalists, Egypt is considered second to Israel in holiness and is referred to as the ‘secondary chariot’ (after the Torah’s description of the chariot in which Yosef rode). Rabbi Benamozegh notes that this Kabbalistic notion parallels early Christian scholarship, where 2nd century scholars like Origen engaged in ranking ancient Gentile greats according to their closeness or distance from Israel.

8.0:
Wine and strong drink you shall not drink, you and your sons with you, when you come into the Tent of Meeting, lest you die – a perpetual state for your generations...
Rabbi Benamozegh offers a detailed interpretation of the Torah’s injunction against the consumption of wine and strong drink.
This passage is understood by Ḥazal to encompass all intoxicating substances, a viewpoint also recognised by 4th century Christian scholar, Jerome. In his writings, Jerome acknowledges the Talmudic interpretation, noting that the Hebrew word שכר refers to any drink that can intoxicate.
Rabbi Benamozegh expands this discussion by citing examples from non-Israelite ancient societies that similarly prohibited the use of intoxicating substances. A notable instance is the Carthaginian law (c. 400 BCE), which forbade the introduction of wine and any intoxicating substance into military camps. This prohibition extended beyond the military context, as it also applied to various segments of Carthaginian society. The law restricted the consumption of wine even by slaves and maidservants, let alone city leaders, including seniors and city officials, throughout their term of service. Moreover, specific regulations governed the behaviour of city leaders and judges, barring them from drinking wine while sitting in judgement. Additionally, when their Senate convened to discuss serious matters or religious decrees, it was stipulated that none of the participants could consume wine on that day. Rabbi Benamozegh notes that these accounts are referenced in the works of 3rd century Greek historian, Eusebius of Caesarea.

1.0:
Speak to the Israelites, saying ‘These are the beasts that you may eat of all the animals that are on the land...
Rabbi Benamozegh explores the nuances of kosher dietary laws, arguing that their purpose transcends mere health preservation.
He highlights how dietary habits significantly vary across cultures. For instance, Arabs commonly consume camel meat, considering it healthy, while some contemporary doctors of his era advocate the nutritional benefits of horse meat. However, both are forbidden to consume according to the Torah. This cultural diversity in dietary preferences underscores that the kosher laws cannot be solely grounded in health concerns.
Rabbi Benamozegh critically evaluates two suggestions made regarding the reasons for the kosher dietary laws by his contemporary, Shadal.
The first notion that Rabbi Benamozegh critiques is that the prohibition to eat certain foods was partly established to differentiate the Israelites from other nations. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this reasoning does not account for the selection of specific animals, rendering them arbitrary. Additionally, many ancient cultures, including their priesthoods, had their own dietary restrictions, making this differentiation not particularly unique.
Rabbi Benamozegh critiques an extension of this reasoning, namely that if the entire world accepted the sovereignty of one God, prohibitions against foods like pork, reptiles, and mice would be unnecessary. In this scenario, there would be no nation to distinguish Israelites from, so it would render these dietary distinctions redundant. This line of thought is concerning to Rabbi Benamozegh, as it closely resembles Christian arguments for abolishing Torah law, focusing merely on faith rather than deeds.
The second rationale that Rabbi Benamozegh contests is the notion that an abundance of laws helps with character refinement (‘tiqqun ha-middot’). He challenges this idea, comparing it to a tyrant who orders servants about for no other reason than to order them. He states that this notion is due to a misunderstanding about a midrash by Rabbi Ḥananya ben Ạqashya, that God wanted to merit Israel by simply increasing the commandments (which, Rabbi Benamozegh notes, is also what Paul says in Colossians II:23, in what Christians call ‘the New Testament’). Rabbi Benamozegh continues: even if one wants to say that by general restraint through the observance of the commandments one will acquire spiritual resilience, that still does not explain why these specific animals were chosen. And more, if this was the reason then why doesn’t the Torah prohibit any indulgence with this command? After all, one can slaughter as many kosher animals as one wants and eat them all day, every day.
Rabbi Benamozegh states that the Torah adopts a principled approach known as ‘summum jus’ in legal terminology, wherein the rigid application of the law without due and careful consideration about the law’s purpose and overall circumstance can yield detrimental consequences. He notes that Ḥazal reflect this principle by stating that anyone who says “I have nothing other than Torah” actually does not have Torah (Yebamot 109b). In other words, one who rigidly adheres to the dietary laws but lives a hedonistic lifestyle is not achieving the goal of those very commandments. Consequently, those attributing the sole purpose of the commandments to general restraint misunderstand the essence. A notable example is observed in Christian ascetic practices, a path that diverges significantly from the tenets of Judaism. Contrarily, Rabbi Benamozegh argues, the Torah permits enjoyment within certain limits, contradicting the idea that its purpose is to enforce stringent self-denial.
At the heart of Rabbi Benamozegh’s own reasoning for these dietary laws is the concept of inherent purity or impurity in different species of animals. He posits that the Israelites, being priests of God, are commanded to abstain from impure species to attain a higher level of sanctity – just as the priests (Kohanim) were commanded. He reinforces this by referencing various Torah verses that connect dietary laws with sanctity and the unique status of the Israelites.
Moreover, Rabbi Benamozegh references Rabbi Naftali Wessely, who suggested that consuming prohibited foods negatively affects the soul. He also references the 11th century Spanish philosopher Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, who suggested that the spiritual or ethical qualities of the food consumed will somehow be incorporated into or affect the person who eats it. Rabbi Benamozegh believes that these approaches broadly align with Kabbalistic teachings emphasising the profound impact of food on both the body and the soul’s connection to the physical form. Further reinforcing his argument, Rabbi Benamozegh contends that the extensive details of laws related to prohibited foods, as taught by the priests, do not relate to bodily health.
Rabbi Benamozegh also draws on the historical context, pointing out that many ancient groups had similar dietary laws with reasons akin to those in the Kabbalah. He supports this claim with reference to Charles François Dupuis’ study on the origin of religions, emphasising that the prohibited foods do not harm the body or intellect/soul but rather affect the ‘nefesh’ that connects the two.
Transitioning into a critique of certain philosophers, Rabbi Benamozegh questions their reluctance to accept the sanctity-based reasons for dietary laws. He challenges readers to either embrace the profound understanding presented or question the assumption that Divine commandments are arbitrary, comparing them unfavourably with the laws of other nations. Rabbi Benamozegh observes how the so-called philosophers, who should be willing to accept the truth, are ironically unwilling to attribute to God any opinion which they themselves are unable to understand. He mockingly calls out this reticence to accept the ‘burden’ of an ‘illogical’ belief, resulting in philosophers not believing what they see, and instead seeing only what they believe.
However, a philosopher who accepts the implications of a divine Torah is correctly believed. Thus, Rabbi Benamozegh concludes by introducing us to the 19th century Jewish philosopher and orientalist Salomon Munk, praising him for recognising what he considers as the true aim of these dietary laws. Munk posited that if Moshe’s intentions were confined to health preservation, he would not have limited his directives to animal consumption. The absence of such comprehensive guidelines in plant consumption suggests that the Torah’s dietary laws aim beyond mere physical well-being. According to Munk, these laws are more likely oriented towards achieving higher levels of sanctity and purity – just as Rabbi Benamozegh argued. Furthermore, Munk’s argument is bolstered by the historical context. He notes that ancient civilisations typically associated purity and impurity only with living beings possessing breath. This distinction was not commonly extended to inanimate objects or plants, barring a few exceptions, such as hyssop and cedar wood, which were used for purification rituals. This historical perspective supports Rabbi Benamozegh’s idea that the Torah’s dietary laws are not primarily about health but about sanctity.

9.0:
And all in the seas and in the brooks that have no fins or scales, of all the swarming creatures of the water and of all the living things that are in the water, they are an abomination for you.
Rabbi Benamozegh explores the laws pertaining to creatures that dwell in water.
He states that the midrash halakha work Sifra (Shemini 3:7) specifically refers to such sea creatures as a ‘siren’, a mythical entity commonly depicted in ancient lore. This mermaid-like ‘siren’ has a dual nature – its upper body resembles a woman while its lower half is akin to a fish. The Sifra, in its analysis, considers whether the corpse of a ‘siren’ imparts ritual impurity in a tent (‘metame b’ohel’), much like the corpse of a human being does.
Rabbi Benamozegh clarifies that Ḥazal’s belief in the existence of the ‘siren’ is not something to be dismissed or ridiculed by the modern reader. Their belief was not born out of ignorance or superstition. He argues that it is important to recognise that in the era of Ḥazal, the testimony of sailors and travellers who claimed to have seen such creatures was taken seriously. These accounts were not just mere folklore but were considered credible observations that merited attention and discussion, even being analysed by the Roman natural philosopher, Pliny. According to Rabbi Benamozegh, our Sages, like people of all eras, tried to make sense of the world around them using the knowledge and resources available at their time.

15.0:
And the ostrich and the night hawk and the seagull and the hawk according to its kind
Rabbi Benamozegh addresses the identification of the word תחמס in our verse.
He references the 17th century Swiss expert on Ashkenazi Jewry, Johannes Buxtorf, who interprets ‘taḥmas’ as the rondini or swallow bird. However, Rabbi Benamozegh notes that there is an alternative interpretation that links ‘taḥmas’ to a crocodile, based on Coptic. This interpretation is supported by reference to 19th century French expert on ancient mythology, Joseph-Daniel Guignaut, in his work Religions de l’Antiquité, where he cites Herodotus’ description of ‘Tachompso’, the ‘Island of Crocodiles’. Rabbi Benamozegh notes the similarity between that word and the ‘taḥmas’ in our verse.

1.0:
Speak to the Israelites, saying, ‘Should a woman quicken with seed and bear a male, she shall be unclean seven days, as in the days of her menstrual unwellness she shall be unclean.
Rabbi Benamozegh expertly merges Talmudic interpretations with the insights of natural philosophers, spanning from ancient times to his own time.
He refers to a discussion in the Talmudic tractate Nidda (3a), which suggests that women who emit seed first are predisposed to conceive male children. This perspective echoes the beliefs of numerous esteemed natural philosophers throughout history. Rabbi Benamozegh highlights this as an example of how Ḥazal often incorporated prevailing scientific knowledge into their exegetical practices, remarking, “Our Sages followed these natural philosophers, as is their way in all matters of human wisdom, to seek shelter in the shadow of the wisdom of their times.”
He further discusses the view as set forth in the Talmud (Nidda 31a-b) that conception is most likely to occur near a woman’s menstrual cycle. There, Rabbi Yiṣḥaq cites the verse in Tehillim (51:7) that states “Behold, I was born in iniquity [Heb. avon]” as the source for this. However, Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees, stating that instead, conception is most likely to occur near immersion, as that same verse states “And in sin [Heb. ‘ḥet’] did my mother conceive me.” The Talmud links the word ‘ḥet’ to purification, based on its usage to refer to the purification of a house stricken with ṣara’at. However, the link from Rabbi Yiṣḥaq’s source to menstruation is less clear.
Rabbi Benamozegh cites the interpretation of 11th century French commentator Rashi, which links the idea of avon to the prohibition on engaging in intercourse close to the expected time of menstruation. Since this is the time that conception is most likely to occur (according to Rabbi Yiṣḥaq), this brings the husband to the avon of engaging in intercourse at this time.
Expressing astonishment at the complex interpretation, Rabbi Benamozegh suggests a more straightforward understanding, linking the equating of menstrual blood with ‘sin’ to the sin of Adam. According to a midrash, this sin of Adam resulted in the curse of menstruation in women.
Concluding his discourse, Rabbi Benamozegh points out the consensus among expert physicians, from Hippocrates in the 5th century BCE to Herman Boerhaave in the 17th century, regarding the high probability of conception around the menstrual period. He underscores the synergy between Talmudic insight and scientific understanding, illustrating how these seemingly disparate fields often converge in their explanations of natural phenomena, especially in the realm of human biology and conception.

2.0:
And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
Rabbi Benamozegh explains the rationale behind the timing of circumcision (berit mila) on the eighth day after birth.
He argues that this practice is grounded in two ancient beliefs, that a newborn was not regarded as a viable or fully created being until the eighth day, and the significance that lay behind the seventh day.
Furthermore, Rabbi Benamozegh draws a parallel with the treatment of animals as stated in Vayiqra 22:27: “When a bull or a sheep or a goat is born, it shall remain seven days with its mother, and from the eighth day and thereafter it shall be accepted as an offering by fire to YHWH.” In other words, the offering of an animal can only take place from the eighth day onwards, after having spent seven days with its mother. He cites a midrash in which Ḥazal liken this law to a king who says that before seeing him, guests must see the matrona (a Latin word meaning an honourable woman) first. The matrona refers to a Shabbat which must pass the newborn animal before it is offered up to God, represented by the king. Rabbi Benamozegh links this passage to the similar requirement of circumcision on the eighth day, in order that the child encounter the matrona of Shabbat before being brought close to God through circumcision.
Returning to the verse about the newborn animal, Rabbi Benamozegh proceeds to address the common misconception that this period before separation from the mother is merely out of compassion. He clarifies that while compassion might be a factor, it is not the primary intention, as we can see from the similarity of practise between it and circumcision, where compassion is irrelevant.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh references similar practices among ancient Greeks, who would not name a child until the seventh day due to the belief that the child was at risk during this initial period. This practice, as he notes, is documented in Aristotelian works and in historical texts on medicine, showing a cross-cultural recognition of the significance of this initial period in a child’s life.

15.0:
And when a man has an emission of seed, he shall bathe his whole body in water and be unclean until evening.
Rabbi Benamozegh unpacks the phrase “emission of seed” (שכבת זרע) by drawing from Shadal’s work, Mishtadel.
Shadal presents two interpretations to explain the meaning of this enigmatic phrase, which literally means ‘the laying down of seed’: firstly, that the semen must be spread on a garment, akin to a person lying down; and secondly, the act of lying down itself. However, Rabbi Benamozegh proposes a different understanding, suggesting a reversal of the two words of the phrase. He posits that the phrase שכבת זרע should be understood as “the semen of lying down” (i.e., זרע השכיבה), indicating semen emitted during marital relations, commonly referred to euphemistically as “lying down”. This interpretation is supported by a verse in Vayiqra 18:20: “And you shall not put your ‘lying down’ into your fellow man’s wife to emit seed to be defiled through her...”
15.1:
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses the ritual of washing with water that follows the emission. He argues that this immersion is not for physical cleanliness, nor is it due to climate conditions, as some have suggested. To substantiate this, he notes that many ancient nations, including the Greeks, practised ritual immersions, even though their climate did not require it. These immersions were integral to ancient religious ceremonies, such as the initiation rites of the Greek Eleusinian mysteries, and other secret rites imitating Bacchus, with references dating back to the era of Homer, from his Iliad.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh cites a “free-thinking researcher” who, though not aligned with religious views, has independently acknowledged a partial truth in his assessment of these practices. The researcher, identified as 19th century French politician-turned-occultist Victor Hennequin, suggests that while the commandments of purity and immersion might serve bodily health, they also signify a deeper reality. He proposes that physical cleanliness symbolises the purity of the soul, thereby linking physical actions with spiritual meanings.

3.0:
A sacral linen tunic he shall wear and linen breeches shall be on his body and with a linen sash he shall gird himself and a linen turban he shall don.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the origins and symbolism of the “sacral linen tunic” worn during religious rites.
He begins by addressing the identification of “bad” (בד), traditionally interpreted as ‘flax’ or ‘linen’. This leads to a discussion of the attire of Egyptian priests, who were also known to wear linen garments, referred to as ‘linigeri’ (Latin for ‘linen-clad’) by ancient scribes. He describes how linen has royal connotations in ancient Greek society too, often associated with nobility and divinity. This comparison underscores a broader point: the universality of certain religious symbols and practices across different cultures, which he calls a general principle of Kabbalah.
Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises the importance of not being astonished by these cultural similarities, suggesting that such comparisons are crucial to understanding the principles underlying religious practices and their investigation. He argues that these connections between different cultures bridge wisdom and faith, creating “peace in the heavens”.
3.1:
The Rabbi further explores the symbolic significance of garments in various ancient cultures. He notes that ancient Greek performers of poetry (rhapsodists) would wear specific colours during their recitations to symbolise different themes: blue for narrating the sea voyages in Homer’s Odyssey and red for the tales of bloodshed in the Iliad. This practice of using attire to symbolise and indicate the nature of service is also found in Jewish tradition, where the priestly garments are imbued with symbols and hints. Rabbi Benamozegh shows that this practice of using attire as a narrative tool is paralleled in Jewish tradition, with prophets like Yeshayahu, Yeḥezkel, and Hoshe’a adopting symbolic actions or appearances to convey deeper messages and directs us to study another of his works entitled Storia degli Esseni, (‘History of the Essenes’).
The commentary further explores the etymology of ‘linen’ and its royal connotations, tracing back to ancient Greek and Egyptian traditions. He suggests that the term ‘ḥorai’, used in Sefer Yeshayahu, refers to linen, and thus Ḥur, son of Miriam, could be based on an Egyptian loanword or translated idea, meaning ‘proper’ and ‘important’, based on the linen-clad priests. Rabbi Benamozegh then anonymously cites one writer, who claims that the name ‘Athens’ was bestowed upon that city by Egyptians, to refer to the linen worn by their dignitaries. He supports this by referencing the verse in Mishle which mentions “dyed Egyptian linen [Heb. eiṭun],” with ‘eiṭun’ an Egyptian loanword from ‘idmy’. He then notes how Athens is protected by the goddess Athena, whose Kabbalistic root is in the sefira of malkhut (associated with femininity and royalty), as is the root of her parallels in Egyptian, Sidonian and Indian mythology. It is no coincidence, then, that the material of linen hints to the sefira of malkhut. This exploration reveals a profound connection between language, material culture, and religious thought. Rabbi Benamozegh ultimately argues that these allegories are deeply rooted in Jewish tradition, stretching back to Moshe and influenced by the customs and teachings of ancient Egypt.
Moving from material culture to linguistic symbolism, Rabbi Benamozegh examines how names and terms in the Tanakh can serve as symbols or signs. For instance, the term ‘yobel’ (Jubilee year) not only refers to the ram’s horn blown during it but also signifies concepts of return and repentance (see below, 23:24). He points out that Ḥazal extended this interpretation by associating the shofar blown on Rosh Hashanah with improving your deeds before God. A similar idea is present in the Talmud’s assertion of the validity of the simanim, eating ‘symbolic’ foods on Rosh Hashanah, based on linguistic similarities. However, Rabbi Benamozegh observes how quick people are to dismiss this kind of symbolism, despite the fact that it is to be found even in the prophets. He discusses how Yirmiyahu’s act of breaking a potter’s jug (a ‘baqbuq’) in front of the elders and senior priests, as commanded by God, serves as a vivid metaphor for destruction (in Hebrew, ‘ubaqoti’) and divine judgement. According to Rabbi Benamozegh, this is true even though the actual etymology of baqbuq has nothing to do with splitting open or destruction, but rather is an onomatopoeia of the sound a liquid makes as it is poured out of a baqbuq. This allegorical approach is consistent with other prophetic visions, such as Amos’ vision of a basket of summer fruit (qayiṣ) symbolising the end (qeṣ) of Israel, again despite their being no etymological link between the two.
3.2:
Rabbi Benamozegh’s commentary also includes an analysis of Egyptian hieroglyphics, noting that an eye (‘i̓rt’) was used to symbolise action or behaviour due to its phonetic similarity to the Egyptian word for ‘to do’ (‘i̓ri̓’). This method of symbolism, he argues, is akin to the allegorical interpretations in our tradition. He sources this from the Museum of Turin’s Illustrated Catalogue of Egyptian Monuments, written by the 19th century Pietro Camillo Orcurti.
Further, he notes that in Arabic, the verb “to say” (qal) originates from the word for “voice” (al-qawl), highlighting a more direct, literal derivation. This is true for the above-mentioned example in Egyptian, where the word i̓ri̓ lent itself to the verb meaning ‘to see’, again a literal derivation. He contrasts this with the more profound connection in Israelite and symbolism, where names and characteristics often have deeper, interconnected meanings.
He also touches upon the Greek language, where the soul is compared to a butterfly, not for their similarity but because of the shared name (‘psichi’). However, Rabbi Benamozegh thinks that there is a greater connection than simply a shared name. He points to the 14th century writer Dante, whom he calls “the great Italian poet”, who referred to human beings as ‘angelica farfalla’, ‘angelic butterflies’, in his Purgatorio. In point of fact, citing Orcurti, he considers these kinds of connections between words to be either due to phonetic similarity (as in Egyptian i̓ri̓ meaning ‘to do’ being written with the symbol for an eye), or due to conceptual similarity. However, as Orcurti further writes, the phonetic similarities, in his mind, ultimately derive from a shared original source. As an example of this second connection, he explains that the Hebrew word for almond (‘shaqed’) is not just connected to, but ultimately derived from its rapid maturation, symbolising swiftness (‘shoqed’). Similarly, the Hebrew word for summer, ‘qayiṣ’ is thought to be derived from ‘qeṣ’ meaning ‘end’, symbolising the culmination of the year. Ultimately, Rabbi Benamozegh concludes that each word must be assessed independently; the words for some items derive from the nature of that item, while some items lend their word to describe other things of a similar nature to that item.

5.0:
And Aharon shall bring forward the offense-offering bull which is his and atone for himself and for his household
Rabbi Benamozegh takes this opportunity to focus on the High Priest (Kohen Gadol).
He notes that Ḥazal traditionally held the view that the High Priest should be married to only one wife. This perspective is further elucidated through historical references. Rabbi Benamozegh mentions Souda, the 10th century encyclopaedia of the ancient Mediterranean world, which highlights that among the Egyptian laws there was a specific prohibition against polygamy for certain individuals. Furthermore, he cites the 1st century ancient Greek historian Diodorus, who specifies that this restriction of marrying only one woman was specifically applicable to priests. He refers the reader to English historian Sharon Turner’s work, Sacred History of the World.

7.0:
And he shall put lots on the two goats, one for YHWH and one for Azazel.
Rabbi Benamozegh’s commentary delves into the multifaceted interpretations of the term עזאזל and its implications in Jewish theology and history.
He begins by resolutely asserting that ‘Azazel’ is unequivocally the name of an evil angelic being, a point he considers indisputable. In contrast, he notes that Shadal suggests that while ‘Azazel’ did indeed originally refer to an evil demon in various cultures, its meaning was adopted by the Israelites to become a metaphor or embodiment for calamity, evil, or destruction, and its original meaning was erased (this is known as semantic bleaching). This transformation can be likened to the modern expression, “What the devil is going on?”, which does not imply a belief in a devil’s involvement but rather signals the recognition of a negative event.
Rabbi Benamozegh challenges Shadal’s interpretation by pointing out that the term ‘Azazel’ is never used elsewhere in the Torah to simply mean ‘bad’ or ‘calamity’. Its exclusive appearance in our verse, specifically in the context of a goat offered to God, is enough for Rabbi Benamozegh to deduce that the goat designated for ‘Azazel’ is considered a pure offering (‘qorban tahor’) commanded by God, for the sake of God. In essence, Rabbi Benamozegh proposes that this offering to ‘Azazel’ aligns with God’s will.
He presents a fascinating juxtaposition from Shemot 34:20, which features the ritual of the redemption of the firstborn donkey by either beheading it (arifa) or redeeming it with a sheep. In both cases, the redemption of the firstborn donkey is an impure offering (qorban tame), used for the purpose of purification and sanctification. Rabbi Benamozegh notes that the choice of beheading over traditional slaughter (sheḥita) should not be surprising to the reader. After all, there are Temple practices where birds are killed through a form of beheading (meliqa) for the purpose of atonement (kappara), as well as the ritual of the ‘egla arufa’, whereby elders of a town decapitate a female cow to atone for an unsolved murder.
Rabbi Benamozegh then raises critical questions about the unique use of the name ‘Azazel’ in the context of the Yom Kippur ritual. He thinks that there are two main problems with Shadal’s interpretation. The first is that were this term to be a general one meaning ‘calamity’, one would expect to see it at least once elsewhere in Tanakh with this meaning. The second problem is that if this word is to be used only once, then the worst place to use it would be the one place where there may actually be potential confusion regarding its original meaning!
Addressing Rabbi Naftali Wessely’s interpretation of Azazel as ‘az azal’ (a combination of ‘azah’ meaning ‘strong’, and ‘zal’ meaning ‘to go’), Rabbi Benamozegh finds this explanation to be far-fetched. Rabbi Wessely had suggested that the term symbolised a ‘strong spirit’ and alluded to a mighty wind that would cast the goat off a mountain, leading to its death. Rabbi Benamozegh criticises this interpretation for its lack of grounding in traditional Jewish exegesis and for straying into the realm of speculative and unusual explanations.
7.1:
He then delves into the broader implications of the term ‘Azazel’ in Hebrew, arguing that if it merely meant ‘evil’, it would not be used in the phrase “to send to Azazel in the wilderness” as the Hebrew language does not typically construct phrases in this manner.
Rabbi Benamozegh links the idea of the ‘Azazel’ to Egypt. He presents a derasha of our Sages in which there is a star (meaning some natural force of some kind) that is called ra’a (evil). This is what is meant when the verse says that רעה נגד פניכם, “ra’a is in front of you”, when the Israelites left Egypt. Now, to the Egyptians, it looked like God himself was punishing them and bringing about these bad punishments. Rabbi Benamozegh directs us to the Greek god Typhon, who was the force of natural disasters, and who was later linked to the Egyptian god ‘Set’, who was god of the desert. He sees from this that the Egyptians thought that a God that brings about natural disasters and then brings his people to the desert, must be this evil god!
Hence the verse, למה יאמרו מצרים לאמר ברעה הוציאם להרוג אותם בהרים, “why should the Egyptians say, ‘as ra’a/evil (Typhon/Set) he brought them out.’”
The discussion expands to the connection between ‘Azazel’ and early Christian sects, like Marcion and his followers, who viewed the God of the Torah, in their eyes the ‘Old’ Testament, as an evil god (or vengeful demiurge). Rabbi Benamozegh suggests that the Talmudic teaching of Rabbi Ḥananya ben Ạqashya, which speaks of God’s desire to merit Israel through having many commandments, counters this negative portrayal of the Torah. Rabbi Ḥananya ben Ạqashya’s source is a verse which reads למען צדקו, “[God desires] for their righteousness”, which Rabbi Benamozegh interprets not as righteousness, but as justification/salvation. This salvation and ultimate justification are achieved through the numerous commandments, not through faith (in Jesus).
Returning to the subject of ‘Azazel’, Rabbi Benamozegh compares the ‘Azazel’ goat with the two birds used in the cleansing ritual for lepers. One bird is sacrificed in the Temple, and the other is released over the field, a practice he sees as analogous to the sending of the ‘Azazel’ goat to the wilderness, although the name ‘Azazel’ is not explicitly mentioned in the bird ritual.
7.2: Rabbi Benamozegh also delves into the evolution of the concept of angels in Jewish tradition. He traces this development from the times of the Patriarchs, where angels were acknowledged but their names were not revealed, through Moshe, who introduced the name ‘Azazel’, and onto later prophets like Yeshayahu and Daniel, who provided more details and names of angels. This progression, according to Rabbi Benamozegh, reflects a shift from the ancients’ preference for concealment and mystery to a later trend towards explicitness and revelation.
7.3: Revisiting the subject of the firstborn donkey, Rabbi Benamozegh observes that the animal of the Egyptian god ‘Set’ is the donkey. He then links ‘Set’ to ‘Satan’ and notes how the Kabbalists consider the donkey to be on the lowest level of tum’a (which incidentally indicates, to Rabbi Benamozegh, that Kabbalah was developing even as the Israelites were in Ancient Egypt). He goes on to mention the idea – present in both Jewish writers and non-Jewish writers – that the Jews are influenced by a negative star (or natural force). This star is identified with kiyyun, or remphan, as per Coptic scholars whom he cites.

21.0:
And the goat shall bear upon it all their transgressions to a remote region, and he shall send off the goat to the wilderness.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the symbolism and deeper meaning of the phrase “to a remote region” (אל־ארץ גזרה).
He connects this concept with his previous writings on the topic of ‘Azazel’, emphasising the significance of the desert as a remote place of exile and spiritual desolation. Rabbi Benamozegh refers to the desert as a traditional dwelling of demons and evil spirits, a theme echoed in various religious and philosophical texts.
Rabbi Benamozegh quotes the 19th century Christian philosopher Vincenzo Gioberti, who elaborates on the association of the desert with evil entities. In Della Filosofia della Rivelazione, Gioberti notes how the Biblical ‘Azazel’, ‘Asmodeus’ from the 2nd century Book of Tobit, and the demons exorcised in Christian tradition are all linked to the desert. This remote and desolate landscape is portrayed as the abode of Satan and evil spirits.
The desert’s connection with Satan is further explored by Gioberti through various cultural and historical lenses. The angel who bound Tobit did so in the desert of Egypt, and in Matthew we read that Satan led Jesus into the desert, as demons seek refuge there after being exorcised. These examples further underline the desert’s symbolic role. Gioberti posits that Satan is often associated with the desert because the desert symbolises desolation and emptiness, qualities that are attributed to Satan.
The commentary then shifts to a philosophical discussion, where Gioberti argues that the desert metaphorically represents a void, or a place devoid of “God’s glory and the light of reason”. This absence of divine presence and rationality renders the desert a fitting dwelling for evil spirits and demons. He then links these to the philosophical concepts of ‘mimesis’ and ‘methexis’. In Platonic terms, the term ‘mimesis’ means imitation or representation but not actually partaking of the essence. This concept is used to suggest that Satan imitates or mimics physical reality, stemming from the goodness of God, rather than embodying its true essence. In contrast, ‘methexis’, meaning participation in the essence of the Platonic forms, is used to denote actual partaking in reality, from which Satan is detached. This philosophical distinction highlights that Satan is seen as a mere imitation of reality, lacking genuine participation in the higher, more profound order of existence. Since the desert is portrayed as a remote, barren, godless place, it becomes an appropriate habitat for Satan, who is disconnected from genuine reality and divine presence. He notes that this concept of imitation is echoed in Kabbalistic teachings, where the monkey is seen as an imitator of man. Consequently, Gioberti depicts Satan as a desert-dwelling hermit, emphasising Satan’s isolation and separation.

3.0:

Rabbi Benamozegh specifies “the entrance of the Tent of Meeting” as the unique site for conducting sacrifices.
While some argue that this locational specification was meant to restrict sacrificial practices due to the unique and confined nature of the designated site, as part of a wider drive to limit and minimise sacrifices in general, Rabbi Benamozegh challenges this perspective with two distinct arguments.
Firstly, he points out that the primary reason for designating a specific place for sacrifices, especially in the desert, was to prevent Israelites from offering sacrifices to demons, rather than limiting the act of sacrifices itself.
Secondly, Rabbi Benamozegh dismisses the idea that the Torah’s intention, in its detailed commandments regarding sacrifices, is to curtail the practice of offering sacrifices. On the contrary, he asserts that the Torah imposes a heavy number of sacrifices for every transgression, whether verbal or in deeds, alongside gifts, vows, and other offerings.
He elaborates that the limitations placed by the Torah are because sacrifices are acceptable and pleasing only if they meet certain conditions and are accompanied by appropriate actions before and after the offering. These conditions ensure that the sacrificial process remains unblemished in thought, speech, and action. The Torah therefore entrusted this responsibility to God’s priests at a designated, recognised place, thereby upholding the purity and sanctity of the sacrifices. If sacrifices lacked defined regulation and location, then people might end up ruining their sacrifices.
He also touches upon the ramifications of deviating from the prescribed sacrificial practices. He asserts that any deviation from any conditions provided by God is ‘aboda zara’ (literally, ‘foreign service’). Whether it is service directly to a foreign god, or serving the God of Israel but in whatever way a person decides, instead of what has been commanded, both are considered ‘aboda zara’.
To bolster his arguments, Rabbi Benamozegh references the views of the 4th century Greek philosopher Plato in Book X of his Laws. Unlike those advocating for the abolition of sacrifices, Plato proposed that sacrifices be limited to a single temple at the city, under the supervision of those knowledgeable in sacrificial rites. This, Plato reasoned, was because the act of sacrifice demands extensive planning, wisdom, and divine intention. Rabbi Benamozegh sees a parallel between Plato’s reasoning and the inner intention of the Torah, emphasising the need for a controlled, respectful approach to sacrificial practices as a reflection of divine wisdom and intention.

13.0:
For the life of all flesh, its blood is in its life, and I say to the Israelite: the blood of all flesh you shall not consume, for the life of all flesh is its blood, all who consume it shall be cut off.
Rabbi Benamozegh engages the prohibition against consuming blood.
He begins his commentary by citing the foremost authority of 15th century Karaite Jewry, the Turkish “Ḥakham” Eliyahu Bashyazi, who raises a point about the inclusion of all forms of blood in this verse.
Bashyazi’s interpretation stems from the specific mention of birds and beasts in another verse, וכל דם לא תאכלו לעוף ולבהמה, seemingly omitting other creatures like fish and locusts. However, “Ḥakham” Bashyazi draws attention to our later verse, which states “the blood of all flesh”, accompanied by the rationale “for the life of all flesh is its blood”. This phrase, according to “Ḥakham” Bashyazi, implies an inclusive interpretation, suggesting that the prohibition against consuming blood extends beyond just birds and beasts to encompass all living creatures, including fish and locusts.
Rabbi Benamozegh identifies two key errors in “Ḥakham” Bashyazi’s interpretation. The first error is in isolating the verse “the blood of all flesh” away from the animals mentioned in the preceding verse, namely beasts and birds. This verse is clearly linked to the previous one, thus delimiting the prohibition on blood to the beasts and birds.
Rabbi Benamozegh now addresses the second error. He argues that the blood of fish and locusts is fundamentally different, and thus not included under the Scriptural term “blood”. He posits that the Torah’s use of the term “blood” does not encompass all forms of life, and the fact that the word “blood” is used by people to refer to both animal blood and fish/locust blood is coincidental, and the two substances do not share the same Scriptural term of “blood”. Expanding on this idea, Rabbi Benamozegh applies the same logic to the material of wool in forbidden mixtures of wool and flax, which the Talmud interprets as specifically referring to ‘sheep’s wool’. In this context, wool and flax are understood based on their common, everyday usage and significance, rather than their specific botanical or zoological distinctions. This approach emphasises the Torah’s focus on the functional and practical aspects of these substances in human life.
13.1:
Rabbi Benamozegh also addresses the grammatical interpretation of the verse. He notes that some grammarians invert the sentence and interpret the phrase as “its life is in its blood”, suggesting that the essence or life of a being is contained in its blood. He challenges this interpretation on two fronts. First, he argues that the Torah’s syntactic order, “for the life of all flesh, its blood is in its life”, indicates that the focus is on what constitutes life, rather than what is inherent in the blood. If the Torah intended to emphasise the blood, it would have been phrased differently.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh references an ancient philosophical idea, quoting 3rd century philosopher Plotinus, to illustrate that the life, or the soul, of a being is the primary essence, and the physical body, including blood, is secondary. He links Plotinus to the Kabbalistic idea that rather than the spiritual essence being contained in the physical body, the physical body is contained in the spiritual essence, specifically in the Kabbalistic concept of the ‘animal soul’ (‘nefesh habehamit’).

17.0:
And a woman with her sister you shall not take to become rivals, to lay bare her nakedness while her sister is still alive.
Rabbi Benamozegh offers a critical examination and refutation of an interpretation presented by the 17th century French theologian Pierre Jurieu, particularly concerning the Sadducees’ stance on polygamy.
Jurieu suggests that the Sadducees interpreted our verse to mean a prohibition against marrying two women at the same time. Jurieu draws an analogy from a different Torah verse found in Shemot 26:3, which discusses the coupling of curtains in the Tabernacle, using the phrase “one with another”, which in Hebrew translates literally to ‘a woman to her sister’. In this context, “one with another” is understood to mean connecting one distinct curtain with another distinct curtain. Jurieu extrapolates this understanding to the verse “a woman with her sister”, interpreting it to mean that just as the curtains are distinct and separate entities joined together, so too the phrase implies a prohibition against marrying one distinct woman while still married to another. In other words, he suggests that the Sadducees read this verse as an implicit prohibition of polygamy.
Rabbi Benamozegh challenges this view, arguing that such an interpretation is fundamentally flawed. He questions the logic behind understanding “with her sister” as referring to every woman. If this were the case, he argues, then how is the prohibition of marrying a woman and her sister derived? Furthermore, he raises the question of why the Torah explicitly prohibits a man from “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter you shall not lay bare” in the preceding verse (18:17) if all women are implied in the prohibition.
Delving deeper, Rabbi Benamozegh addresses the specific language used in the two verses in question. He notes the difference in the wording of the prohibition in 18:18, which focuses on “you shall not take to become rivals” rather than the wording in 18:17, which focuses on not laying bare “the nakedness of a woman and her daughter”. From this, perhaps Jurieu also inferred a general prohibition against polygamy. However, Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this specific phrasing is used because the prohibition differs from other forbidden relations. He explains that unlike other relations where marriage is never permitted, a man may indeed marry his wife’s sister after his wife’s death. Therefore, the Torah uses the language of “taking to become rivals” to indicate that it is only forbidden to marry the sister during the wife’s lifetime, not after her death.
Rabbi Benamozegh concludes by dismissing the opinion of the Sadducees as presented by Jurieu, thereby nullifying the argument against polygamy.

24.0:
And the land became defiled, and I made a reckoning with it for its iniquity, and the land spewed out its inhabitants.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the nuanced use of allegorical language in the Torah. He begins by addressing the phrase “and the land became defiled” interpreting it in a manner that unveils the nature of sin and its consequences.
He challenges the notion of simplifying complex Torah verses such as this by labelling them as allegories, as Shadal does here. After all, how can a land be “defiled”? He argues that this approach to allegorise everything can be reductive, potentially leading to a dismissal of the deeper search for truth.
This perspective is crucial in understanding the distinction between different books in the Jewish canon. For example, he contrasts the usage of allegory in the Torah with its prevalence in the Prophetic books (Nebi’im and Ketubim). In the Five Books of Moshe (Torah), allegorical expressions are sparingly used. To support this, Rabbi Benamozegh refers to Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra’s responses to the Karaites who regarded tefillin as a mere allegory, and not a physical ritual. There, Ibn Ezra emphasises that Moshe’s teachings in the Torah do not follow the same pattern of parables and allegories found in Mishle, attributed to King Solomon.
Rabbi Benamozegh notes that Moshe’s language frequently adopts the kind of terminology seen in our verse when discussing the sin of the land and its atonement. He cites Bemidbar 35:33, a verse that suggests the land can only be purified of bloodshed through the blood of the perpetrator. The verse conveys the idea that the sin of murder defiles the land, and the only way to atone for this sin is through the punishment of the murderer.
Thus, he asks: If these are indeed simply allegorical, as Shadal alleges, why does Moshe resort to this allegorical style only in this specific context? Instead, Rabbi Benamozegh proposes that Moshe’s choice of words in these instances aligns with the opinion of the sages of Kabbalah.
