According to them, sin has a pervasive effect on all aspects of reality, with a particularly profound impact on the land in which those who commit the sins dwell. This effect is even more significant in the Land of Israel, viewed as the Divine abode, a chosen dwelling place, and the foundational stone from which the world originated. Therefore, Moshe’s choice of phrasing in these contexts, such as ‘defilement’ of the land, underscores the gravity and spiritual reality of sin’s impact, especially in a significant land like Israel.

3.0:
Do not turn to idols or make molten gods for yourselves. I am YHWH your God.
Rabbi Benamozegh offers a thorough exploration of the term “idols” (אלילים) in the Torah. He engages with various interpretations, delving into the linguistic roots and theological implications.
Rabbi Benamozegh first examines Rabbi Naftali Wessely’s explanation of the word “idols” (האלילים). Rabbi Wessely suggests that the term is derived from a reduplication of אַל (‘al’, meaning ‘not’) which is interpreted as אַלַילים (‘alilim’), connoting the ultimate non-existence, making this a fitting term for idols.
Within Rabbi Wessely’s explanation, Rabbi Benamozegh further explores the possibility that the term אלילים originates from יללה (‘yellah’, meaning ‘wailing’ or ‘crying’), similar to the word אללי (‘alelai’). This interpretation aligns with the term עצבים (‘aṣavim’, also meaning ‘idols’), rooted in עצב (‘aṣav’, meaning ‘sorrow’ or ‘distress’), paralleling the Greek term ‘eidolon’, which signifies sorrow and worry. This linguistic connection underlines the emotional and spiritual anguish associated with idol worship. Although, in contrast, Rabbi Benamozegh notes the term תרפים (‘terafim’), which connotes ‘healing’, presenting a different aspect of the idolatry discourse.
Rabbi Benamozegh also discusses the term אליל (‘elil’) as a compound of אַל (‘al’, meaning ‘not’) and אֵל (‘el’, meaning ‘god’), similar to לא אל (‘lo el’, meaning ‘not god’). He cites Debarim 32:21 to reinforce this point: “They provoked Me with an ungod (בלא אל), they vexed Me with their empty things. And I, I will provoke them with an unpeople (בלא עם) with a base nation I will vex them.” These verses metaphorically relate idolatry to something unGodly, or ‘not God’.
3.1: Moreover, Rabbi Benamozegh critically engages with 18th century Czech Rabbi Shelomo Yehuda Rapoport, who discusses אלל (‘alal’, meaning withered or insubstantial pieces of meat) mentioned in the Mishna. He celebrates that his interpretation aligns with that of Rabbi Rapoport, linking the idols to the ‘yelala’ mentioned above. However, he respectfully disagrees with Rabbi Rapoport’s second interpretation, that links the reduplicated אל אל to ideas of shame.
3.2: Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh touches upon a possibly overlooked aspect of idol names, suggesting that atheism and idol worship are fundamentally similar in nature and purpose. He refers to just such a position identified by 18th century Scottish Enlightenment philosopher David Hume in his Natural History of Religion. He posits that אֵל אַל (‘el al’) is named to reflect the idol worshipper’s state as one without a true god, highlighting a profound spiritual void.

17.0:
You shall not take vengeance and you shall not harbour a grudge against the members of your people. And you shall love your fellow man as yourself. I am YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh elucidates the profound ethical teachings embedded within this famous verse.
He emphasises that the term “fellow man” (לרעך) extends beyond the members of one’s community, embracing all human beings. This interpretation is grounded in the absence of a specific reference to “the members of your people” (לבני עמך) after it, which was there in the previous line. This signifies a universal application of the commandment to love your fellow human, irrespective of their background or conviction.
Rabbi Benamozegh underscores the significance of this commandment by linking it to the treatment of the sojourner (גר) within a community. He draws attention to a later related verse, “the sojourner who resides with you shall be to you as one of your natives; you shall love him as yourself, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (Vayiqra 19:34). This verse serves as a reminder of the Israelites’ own experience as sojourners in Egypt, fostering empathy and compassion towards others residing among them. The reference to Egypt is crucial, as it highlights a parallel between the Israelites’ experience there and the status of the sojourner who, while not obliged to follow all the laws of the Israelite community, is still deserving of love.
Rabbi Benamozegh goes on to refute a potential misunderstanding that the term ‘sojourner’ (גר) refers solely to converts who have embraced all commandments. He clarifies that the ‘sojourner’ mentioned is not necessarily close to the Israelite community but is recognised and respected due to their shared residence. In the words of Rabbi Benamozegh, “just as the Israelites did not keep the Egyptian Torah, so this sojourner does not need to keep the Torah of Israel...” He goes on to state that the command to love the ‘sojourner’ as oneself (in 19:34) is linked to the expectation that they adhere to the seven Noaḥide laws, the set of universal moral laws.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh draws a beautiful parallel between ethical and ritualistic commandments in the Torah. He admires the immediate juxtaposition of “and you shall love your fellow as yourself”, a weighty ethical command, with “you shall not let your cattle mate with a different kind” and “do not sow your field with two kinds of seed”, which are seemingly lighter ritualistic laws. This juxtaposition, in his view, illustrates that all commandments, whether ethical or ritualistic, hold equal importance and are interconnected within the Divine wisdom, which transcends human understanding. This equal valuation of commandments is a testament to God’s wisdom, which perceives the interconnectedness of all aspects of reality.

25.0:
Do not eat over the blood. Do not divine and do not perform augury.
Rabbi Benamozegh interprets this verse in the context of ancient idolatrous practices.
He notes that it refers to a custom among idol worshippers who would gather on mountains, create a pit, slaughter an animal, and pour its blood into the pit. They believed that by doing this, they could summon the dead and request favours or guidance from them. He notes that this ritual is referenced in the popular works of 18th century natural historian, Noel-Antoine Pluche.
Rabbi Benamozegh further explains that the phrase “do not eat over the blood” is translated in the Septuagint as “do not eat over the mountains”. This supports the idea that the verse is specifically addressing the practice of conducting rituals on mountains, a common venue for such blood-based idolatrous rites. Rabbi Benamozegh cites further evidence of this interpretation from the prophet Yeḥezkel, who also alludes to these mountain-based idolatrous practices in Yeḥezkel 18:6 and 18:15, when stating that a righteous person “did not eat upon the mountains”.
Rabbi Benamozegh notes that Ḥazal were aware of the link between the ritual performed on the mountains and the summoning of one’s ancestors, as they link the term ‘mountains’ with Israel’s ancestors. In Sanhedrin 81a, Rab Aha presents a homiletic interpretation of the abovementioned verse from Yeḥezkel (18:6), rendering “he did not eat upon the mountains” as ‘he did not eat due to the merit of his fathers’. In other words, Rab Aha states that this verse in Yeḥezkel is not meant to be simply taken as face value, because merely avoiding eating on a mountain is not enough to qualify someone as righteous. Instead, the expression of not eating upon the mountains is explained as an allusion to the fact that the individual did not rely on the merit of his forefathers for his righteousness. Eating on the mountains is here a metaphor for deriving sustenance or virtue from the deeds of one’s ancestors. The righteous person stands on his own merit and righteousness. This Talmudic derasha shifts the focus from the full-fledged idolatrous practices in which the ancestors are summoned to an appeal towards ancestral merit.
25.1:
The commentary also touches on related practices that were forbidden by Ḥazal, such as slaughtering animals in vessels or pits, which were reminiscent of idolatrous rituals. This was likely informed by their knowledge of idolatrous practices, as described in various sources like the Talmud (Ḥullin 2:45) and Rambam in Hilkhot Sheḥita.
Furthermore, Rabbi Benamozegh brings in a comparison from Greek mythology, specifically referencing Homer’s account of Ulysses. In Homer’s story, Ulysses performs a similar ritual to communicate with the spirit of Tiresias during his journey back to Ithaca. This ritual involves slaughtering an animal and using its blood to summon the spirits, with Ulysses standing on his sword, ready to ward off the unwanted spirits until Tiresias’ spirit arrives. This is an example of the idolatrous practices described earlier.
Lastly, Rabbi Benamozegh references a 2nd century book by the Roman satirist, Lucian. In this book, he describes a descent to the underworld, killing of sheep and using their blood in a ritual involving a pit, with a magician invoking demons. This historical reference further illustrates the widespread nature of these idolatrous practices across different cultures and eras.
25.2:
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses two words in the second half of our verse: “divination” (seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means) and “augury” (similar to seeking omens).
He explains that Ḥazal identified specific types of diviners who use weasels and birds (Sanhedrin 66a). He suggests that divination in ancient times was known as ‘auspicio et augurio’, which is Latin for ‘by auspice and augury’. The etymology of these words equates to ‘by the divination of birds and other omens’, and it reflects a deep-rooted ancient belief that the will of the gods and the future could be understood through careful observation and interpretation of various signs in the natural world. Rabbi Benamozegh explains that both of these Latin words hint at the use of birds, as Ḥazal correctly identified.
This point is supported by a reference to the 16th century surgeon Ludovic Nunez, who considers ‘auspice’ as being the observation of birds, their flight patterns, and vocalisations. Rabbi Benamozegh also adds 7th century theologian Isidore of Seville’s definition of ‘augurio’ as relating to what birds carry. Rabbi Benamozegh proposes that the Latin phrase ’avium garria’ (meaning ‘the chirping of birds’), might have originated from this practice.
Rabbi Benamozegh also delves into the cultural significance of bird divination in Egypt, a region known for its proficiency in this art. He notes that the Arabic term for seeking omens is the word ‘tair’, which translates to ‘bird’.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh references the Zohar’s examples of Jewish involvement in bird divination, even though the Zohar agrees with the Talmud’s interpretation that it is forbidden as a consequence of this verse.

27.0:
No gash for the dead shall you make in your flesh, and no tattoo shall you make on yourselves. I am YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh provides a comprehensive understanding of the cultural and historical context of engraving the skin and tattooing, linking these practices to various customs across different civilisations.
He begins by noting that our verse’s prohibition of both gashing/cutting the flesh and tattooing/engraving the flesh likely indicates a shared underlying reason. He cites an example from the Eskimos in the Americas where tattooing is a form of signalling that they are in a state of mourning, citing an article in the Revue Britannique.
Rabbi Benamozegh expands the discussion by noting that tattooing has been used for multiple purposes across cultures: for beauty, health, religious devotion, desire, hatred, joy, and mourning. He states that this popularity across all eras is also referenced in an article from a popular Italian magazine of his time, II Politecnico.
He explains the term ‘tatuaggio’ in his native Italian, derived from ‘tattoo’ in Polynesian, meaning ‘strike after strike’. He observes that this is similar to the Hebrew term קעקע, implying ‘removal after removal’. This description conveys the idea of a permanent mark made by cutting or piercing the skin, possibly with added colour. He states that this is also the opinion of Ḥazal (Makkot 3:6).
Rabbi Benamozegh continues by discussing how different nations used tattoos as identity markers. He gives examples of the ancient Thracians (South-East Europe) and Parthians (Greater Persia) who tattooed hieroglyphic-like images on their bodies, and the Romans who marked their soldiers physically for identification.
Lastly, Rabbi Benamozegh touches upon the religious and idolatrous aspects of tattooing in ancient civilisations, where people marked their flesh using iron and fire with symbols dedicated to idols, as a sign of devotion and protection. This practice, he implies, contrasts with the monotheistic principles of the Torah, which may be the underlying reason for the prohibition in this verse.

30.0:
Do not turn to the ghosts, and of the familiar spirits do not inquire to be defiled through them. I am YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh presents us with his approach to necromancy and wizardry.
He starts by powerfully stating that this verse serves as “a piercing and descending force into the abyss” to uproot those who argue that practices like necromancy and wizardry are mere vanities that lack any real substance or benefit. They believe, he states, that the Torah’s prohibition of these practices is based solely on the fact that they are not real.
Rabbi Benamozegh, in a characteristically Kabbalistic take, challenges this interpretation by pointing out that the verse explicitly links the prohibition to the impurity inherent in these practices. This assertion is crucial because it shifts the focus from the supposed lack of substance in necromancy and wizardry to the moral and spiritual contamination they entail. According to Rabbi Benamozegh, the Torah’s forbiddance of these practices is not because they are unsubstantial but because they are impure.
He cites the Kabbalah, which also views these practices as spiritually harmful. Rabbi Benamozegh underscores the severity of this issue by questioning how opponents of this view would respond to such a clear and emphatic statement from the Torah. He implies that the opponents, who dismiss necromancy and wizardry as harmless vanities, are confronted with a direct contradiction from the Torah itself, which categorically states the impurity and therefore the forbidden nature of these practices.

31.0:
Before a gray head you shall rise, and you shall defer to an elder and revere your God. I am YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises that the term “elder” (זקן) is symbolic of wisdom rather than just age.
This interpretation, provided by Ḥazal, also aligns with the customs of ancient societies, where wisdom was highly esteemed and often associated with age.
Rabbi Benamozegh illustrates this point by referencing a dialogue between the wise men of Egypt and the Greek philosopher, Solon. The Egyptians said, “Solon, Solon, you Greeks are youths, there is not an old man among you, because you do not have wisdom that has whitened your hair with many days”. This interaction, depicted in Plato’s Timaeus, underscores the association of wisdom with age in ancient cultures.
Despite this focus on wisdom, Rabbi Benamozegh notes that the elderly, regardless of their wisdom, were respected in these societies. This emphasises the agreement of the Torah with contemporaneous ancient practises. He cites the city of Lacedaemon in ancient Greece as a notable example. There, the elderly were honoured in public spaces like theatres or circuses, with everyone standing in their presence. However, this honour was conditional on their societal contribution, as illustrated by a story shared by the ancient Greek philosopher Plutarch, about an elderly bachelor who did not receive the same respect since he had not contributed to the next generation.
31.1:
Rabbi Benamozegh states that this concept is prevalent in our own tradition, as the word זקן is often synonymous with a wise man, irrespective of his physical age. This wisdom is derived from the ancient traditions of Israel, making even the young, if knowledgeable, ‘elderly’ in terms of wisdom.
Rabbi Benamozegh brings in supporting example from Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, who stated that the term זקן refers to the Midianite kings (Bemidbar 22:4). Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this connecting of ‘elders’ to ‘kings’ was not based on their age but on their greatness, leadership, and righteousness. He complements this point by noting that the Talmud (Gittin 62a) refers to our wise Rabbis as ‘kings’.
He notes that this usage extended to the Romans, as their legislative body was termed ‘senatus’, deriving from ‘senex’ meaning ‘old’. indicating a respect for wisdom and experience in governance.

33.0:
Like the native among you shall be the sojourner who sojourns with you, and you shall love him like yourself, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. I am YHWH your God.
Rabbi Benamozegh offers an insightful interpretation of the term “native” (אזרח) as mentioned in this verse. He follows Ḥazal’s lead, in that the term is understood to refer to the original Israelites, the inhabitants of the land of Israel, as opposed to converts.
Rabbi Benamozegh points out that there has been an alternate interpretation of this term, proposed by the 19th century Italian scholar, Rabbi Yiṣḥaq Reggio. Rabbi Reggio believed that אזרח (“native”) referred to a type of convert, particularly the Canaanite residents who converted. However, Rabbi Benamozegh argues against this view, suggesting that it’s a recurring misconception that has been slightly modified and popularised by others. He states that the earliest proponent of this alternate view came from Christian philosophy, which postulated that two types of ‘converts’ left Egypt with the Israelites. The first group comprised original Egyptians, while the second included the tax lords and landowners who had enslaved other Egyptians. These groups, according to that interpretation, accompanied the Israelites during the Exodus.
Rabbi Benamozegh critiques this interpretation, asserting that Moshe, in the context of אזרח was not referring to these converts who journeyed with them through the desert. Instead, Moshe’s use of the term was prophetic, envisioning the time when the Israelites would settle in Canaan. In this future context, “native” referred to the Israelites who would be born in the Promised Land, while “sojourner” (גר) would refer to those from other nations who embraced the Covenant of Israel.

1.0:
And to the Israelites you shall say: ‘Every man of the Israelites and of the sojourners who sojourns in Israel who gives of his seed to Molekh is doomed to die. The people of the land shall stone him.
Rabbi Benamozegh explores the specificities of the idolatrous practice to offer a child to Molekh, a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice.
1.1:
He references Ḥazal’s careful distinction when commenting on the verse, that the directive applies to those “of his seed and not all his seed” (Sanhedrin 64b). This derasha indicates that if one passed all one’s children through the fire, that person would be exempt from the punishment of idolatry. This is due to the practise of sacrificing only one child to Molekh, hence the prohibition on idolatry applies to offering only of his seed, and not all his seed. However, Rabbi Benamozegh notes that Ḥazal did not bring a proof for this assertion. Therefore, he draws a parallel with a custom documented in India, as described by 18th century German archaeologist, Georg Creuzer. According to Creuzer, during certain festivals, priests would sacrifice one man, one horse, and one ox. Rabbi Benamozegh uses this example to suggest that these acts might be similar to what is being condemned in our verse, where only one son is sacrificed.
Additionally, Rabbi Benamozegh notes that Ḥazal had a deeper insight into the nature of this idolatry, as it was more prevalent during their times. The evidence suggests that human sacrifices for idolatry were still performed in the Roman Empire as late as the year 424. This context would allow for Ḥazal’s more profound understanding of the verse and the nature of the specific condemnation of idolatrous practices it entails.

2.0:
And as for Me, I shall set My face against the man and cut him off from the midst of his people, for he has given of his seed to Molekh so as to defile my sanctuary and to profane My sacred name.
Rabbi Benamozegh begins his analysis of this verse by questioning the apparent redundancy of this punishment, as it was already stated in the previous verse that such a person “shall be put to death; the people of the land shall pelt the person with stones.”
Rabbi Benamozegh clarifies that this verse is explicating the concept of “cutting off” or “karet” (כרת) – a punishment that extends beyond physical death.
He emphasises two key insights: firstly, that the soul is inherently eternal and only ceases to be so if it is “cut off”. This concept underscores the gravity of “karet”, as it is not merely a physical demise but an obliteration of the eternal soul. Secondly, he reiterates that “karet” is indeed a spiritual consequence, inflicted post-mortem.
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses the phrase “from the midst of his people” in our verse, in the context of death. He draws a contrast between the righteous and the wicked in their death. For the righteous such as Abraham, Ya’aqob, Yiṣḥaq, and others, we see phrases such as “he shall be gathered unto his people” (ויאסף אל עמיו), and “you shall go to your fathers in peace”, implying a peaceful transition and reunion with ancestors after physical death. This, Rabbi Benamozegh argues, is not a reference to physical burial, as illustrated by Abraham who was buried in Hebron, far from his forefathers.
In stark contrast to being “gathered unto” their people, the wicked are described as being “cut off” from the midst of their people. Rabbi Benamozegh interprets this as a lack of peace or tranquillity in the afterlife. Unlike the righteous, who find rest and unity with their ancestors, the wicked are subjected to a form of eternal unrest and isolation, separated from their people even in death.
2.1:
Rabbi Benamozegh then turns his attention to another phrase in the verse, “to defile My sanctuary”. He posits that the sanctuary in this context is not limited to the physical Temple, but rather encompasses a broader conceptualisation. This includes the land of Israel, the Jewish people as the chosen people, and the Divine presence that resides among them. Rabbi Benamozegh appreciates a similar interpretation by Rashi. He acknowledges that while Rashi’s interpretation is focused on the collective of Israel, a deeper, more mystical understanding can be gleaned from it, which aligns with the principles of Kabbalah. Rabbi Benamozegh suggests that a discerning reader, with an appreciation for the mystical, would recognise the Kabbalistic undertones in Rashi’s words.
This interpretation serves to underscore the profound sacredness of the Jewish people and their land, elevating them to the status of a sanctuary in the eyes of God. He criticises Shadal’s interpretation, that this does indeed refer to defiling the Temple, as one who sacrifices their child to Molekh is indicating that they view the Temple service – which uses only animals, not humans – as inferior. Rabbi Benamozegh views this interpretation as ‘forced’ in order to deny the Kabbalah.

11.0:
If a man lies with his daughter-in-law, both of them shall be put to death; they have committed incest, and their blood is upon them.
Rabbi Benamozegh focuses on the meaning of the phrase “their blood is upon them” (דמיהם בם).
He begins by referencing Haggahot Maimuniyot, the 13th century Ashkenazi gloss to Rambam’s Mishneh Torah. In the glosses on the laws of mourning, it is stated there that one who finds a murdered person should bury them as they are found (i.e. while their “blood” is still “upon them”), without shrouds or even removing their shoes. The Maharil, a 14th century Ashkenazi scholar, states that this practice is paralleled concerning the burial of women who die in childbirth.
Rabbi Benamozegh points out that there does not seem to be a source for this in the Torah, nor in the Talmud or midrash. However, he brings in the early Christian theologian and historian, Jerome of Stridon, who translated the Torah for Christians, and who Rabbi Benamozegh suggests was known to have been taught by “one of the Sages of Israel, perhaps one of the Amor’aim [who] deviated from the peshat.” Jerome appears to have deviated from the simple meaning of the verse in his translation by opining that after being put to death, the incestuous pair should be buried without washing, a practice that later authorities also mentioned. This interpretation seems to align with the practice concerning women in childbirth, where it is feared that perhaps the rebi’it of blood through which the soul departs has already been absorbed into her clothes, and so the clothes must be buried with her. This concern was rooted in an ancient idea that a significant portion of a person’s life force or soul is associated with their blood.
Rabbi Benamozegh then proposes that Jerome might not have recognised the interpretation given by Ḥazal, rather understanding the verse in its simplest form – that the slain lie in their blood. Through this discussion, Rabbi Benamozegh acknowledges the possibility of an ancient source for the opinion of later decisors, suggesting that Jerome likely learned this interpretation from an Amora and did not conceive it independently. This hypothesis is based on the understanding that such an interpretation, deviating from the plain meaning, would not have occurred to Jerome without external influence.
Ultimately, Rabbi Benamozegh argues that Jerome’s interpretation provides evidence that oral traditions continued to evolve and become rooted in our nation even after the sealing of the Talmud. These traditions, having taken root in popular practise, may have been unknown in origin to those who then inquired about them, attempting to find a source. Alternatively, perhaps the later authorities aligned their opinions with those of earlier Sages even unknowingly, thus continuing a unified tradition of interpretation stemming from the same source.

13.0:
And a man who takes a woman and her mother, it is depravity. In fire shall he and they be burned, so that there be no depravity in your midst.
Rabbi Benamozegh challenges Shadal’s interpretation of this verse. According to this verse, in a case where a man has relations with a woman and then her mother, both women are put to death. Shadal explains that the first woman is put to death only if she knows that this man has had relations with her mother, and continues to remain with him and engage in relations.
Rabbi Benamozegh fails to understand what prompted Shadal to depart from the interpretation provided by the Sages (Yebamot 94b). Granted, he wished to explain what the sin of the first woman was, but the Sages limited this verse in multiple ways, for example by stating that the man and only the second woman are put to death.
Rabbi Benamozegh raises multiple questions attacking Shadal’s position. He wonders why the wife should be punished for her husband’s actions, especially considering she was lawfully married to him first. Why should she leave the marriage when she was married correctly? Further, why should she be punished for something that is not within her control, namely divorcing her husband? And if she were to abstain from intimacy with him, causing him to divorce her but without having to pay her ketuba, why should she forfeit her rights to her ketuba simply because he sinned?
The commentary also delves into the timing of the punishment. Rabbi Benamozegh points out that according to Shadal’s interpretation of the text, the husband and both women are subject to the death penalty immediately upon their wrongful union. If this is the case, why is the first wife also liable to punishment, when she has not had any time to ‘remain’ with him? If you were to respond to that by claiming that the execution is indeed to take place only after some time has elapsed and the first woman has remained with him, then that fundamental piece of information is lacking from the Torah’s description! Rabbi Benamozegh therefore rejects Shadal’s understanding in favour of Ḥazal’s commuting of the punishment.

15.0:
And a woman who approaches any beast to couple with it, you shall kill the woman and the beast. They are doomed to die. Their bloodguilt is on them.
Rabbi Benamozegh explores this injunction which, on its surface, simply discusses the punishment for bestiality. This verse, however, is delved into deeply to extract broader theological and ethical implications.
Rabbi Benamozegh notes the inclusion of the animal in the punishment (דמיהם בם) which, at first glance, might seem perplexing given that animals, lacking free will and moral discernment, cannot be held accountable for their actions in the same way humans can. This observation leads him to question the rationale behind such a decree and to explore the deeper meanings and implications behind these words.
He argues that this passage suggests a belief in the transmigration of souls (‘gilgul neshamot’), a concept found within the Kabbalistic tradition. According to this belief, souls are reincarnated through various forms of existence, including human and animal forms, as part of their spiritual journey and purification process. Rabbi Benamozegh implies that if animals could be subject to Divine punishment, it might hint at the presence of a soul or spiritual essence capable of moral judgement and, subsequently, deserving of punishment or reward.
He criticises those who interpret the text superficially and interpret the Torah's commandments purely on ethical or moral grounds. He suggests that such approaches underestimate the intelligence and spiritual capacity of the people. He argues that the Torah does not need to resort to falsehoods or fabrications to convey its truths and that to suggest otherwise is to undermine the Torah's integrity and the depth of its teachings.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh addresses the nuances of capital punishment, indicating that the phrase דמיהם בם is not consistently used throughout the Torah to imply that guilt lies exclusively with the individual (or animal) in question. Rather, it can also instruct on the manner of execution, as understood by the Sages.

0.0:
And YHWH said to Moshe, “Say to the priests, the sons of Aharon, and say to them, ‘For no dead person among his kin shall he be defiled...
Rabbi Benamozegh notes that the Torah’s instruction for priests not to defile themselves by mourning the dead resonates with Platonic philosophy.
According to Rabbi Benamozegh, Plato, a 5th century BCE Greek figure of great renown among ancient philosophers and considered by Rabbi Benamozegh as a kindred spirit to Jewish thought, shared a similar viewpoint. In his works, Plato asserted that priests should abstain from participating in mourning or eulogies. However, he made an exception for a figure known as the Censor, whom he referred to as the “judge of judges”. In Platonic thought, this could be likened to a supreme moral authority.
Rabbi Benamozegh draws a parallel between this Platonic exception and a notable event in Jewish history as noted by Ḥazal - the passing of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, which led to the cessation of priesthood. He interprets this event as having a profound significance in Jewish tradition, akin to the passing of a supreme moral authority. The cessation of the priesthood is seen as a symbolic event marking a significant transition in Judaism.

3.0:
These are the fixed times of YHWH, sacred convocations which you shall call in their fixed time.
Rabbi Benamozegh focuses on the significance of the word “them” (אתם) in this context.
He notes that the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 25a) interprets the word “them” to imply that the festivals (“mo’adim”) can be proclaimed even in cases of error. Rabbi Benamozegh expresses his surprise at discovering that the 10th century Rabbenu Aḥai Gaon derived the same law from alternative words in our verse, the words “convocations” and “you shall call”. He notes his uncertainty about whether Rabbenu Aḥai’s interpretation has its roots in the Talmud or the Baraitot unavailable to us.
Rabbi Benamozegh then contemplates the possibility of using Rabbenu Aḥai Gaon’s different part of the verse to support the law, which we have as a matter of tradition, over and against using the Talmud’s source. He writes that if we cannot find the alternative source anywhere else, then we may accept it as long as it makes more sense to us. This approach, he notes, was also followed by other eminent Sepharadi scholars, Rambam and Rabbenu Ḥananel ben Ḥushiel.
Rabbi Benamozegh uses this law, that the calendar may be fixed even in error, to highlight the national court’s authority in determining the calendar. This shows that the proclamation of festivals is dependent on human decision-making. In support of this, Rabbi Benamozegh mentions Rabbi Naftali Wessely’s commentary on Sefer Vayiqra, which aligns with Rabbenu Aḥai’s interpretation, but does not acknowledge its source.

4.0:
In the first month on the fourteenth of the month at twilight a Passover offering to YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh explains that according to Ḥazal, the term “twilight” (ערבים) commences from the moment the sun starts its descent towards the horizon.
Rabbi Benamozegh further reinforces this interpretation by drawing parallels with European linguistic customs. He notes that in many European languages, the term for evening, (‘sera’) is used to denote the time-period starting from midday. This cross-cultural observation adds an additional layer of credibility to the interpretation that ‘twilight’ in the Jewish tradition begins from the afternoon.

20.0:
And on this very day you shall call a sacred convocation – it will be for you – no task of work shall you do, an everlasting statute in all your dwelling places for your generations.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the profound connections between the Festival of Harvest and the broader historical and cultural practices surrounding the giving of the Torah.
He begins by highlighting a recurring theme in the Written Torah, which subtly suggests that the Festival of Harvest coincides with the day of the giving of the Torah. Rabbi Benamozegh believes that this linkage is not merely a coincidence but is deeply entrenched in ancient traditions. Specifically, he states that this connection between agriculture and lawgiving finds echoes in other cultures. This perception stems from a belief that agriculture’s inventor also laid the foundations of law.
An example given is from ancient Greece, where the Festival of Ceres, goddess of agriculture was celebrated during the harvest season and was not just an agricultural festivity. It also commemorated the proclamation of their religious laws. Greeks believed that Ceres, revered as the goddess who bestowed upon mankind the gift of agriculture, was also the legislator for the people of Eleusis and Athens. Consequently, the Greeks referred to these celebratory days as ‘Thesmophoria’, directly translating to the ‘Bearing of the Law’!
Further exploring this cultural interplay, Rabbi Benamozegh references the Roman adaptation of this festival, known as ‘palilie’. The term ‘palilie’, according to Noël-Antoine Pluche, originates from ‘pelilim’ or ‘peliliya,’ – Hebrew for ‘law’ or ‘statute’. The Latin term ‘caerimonia,’ commonly used to denote religious services in general (‘ceremony’, in English), is said to be derived from the aforementioned ‘Ceres’, the founder of these harvest festival rituals. Rabbi Benamozegh writes that this aspect is acknowledged by 14th century physician Rabbi Yiṣḥaq ben Moshe HaLevi (also known as Profiat Duran).

23.0:
Speak to the Israelite people saying, in the seventh month on the first of the month, you shall have a sabbath, a commemoration with horn blast, a sacred convocation.
The verse is interpreted as a symbolic act commemorating the creation of the world.
Rabbi Benamozegh draws a parallel with Passover, where remembrance is centred on the Exodus from Egypt (Shemot 12:14), a stage which he refers to as “the creation of Israel”. This connection is crucial as it links the act of remembrance to foundational historical events.
Rabbi Benamozegh addresses a key question: why are certain fundamental concepts, like the creation of the world, not explicitly mentioned in the Written Torah? He provides a compelling answer rooted in the purpose and audience of the Torah. He explains that the Written Torah is primarily oriented towards the people of Israel, focusing on their national story and identity. This focus means that universal themes, such as the creation narrative, are not the central subjects of the Written Torah. Instead, these themes find their place in the Oral Torah, which encompasses both the main beliefs that were known to people before Moshe, and those that Moshe himself received directly from God.
Delving deeper, Rabbi Benamozegh highlights that the Written Torah is not just about the story of Israel, but it is also a practical guide for the nation in terms of deeds and actions. This is a crucial point because it underscores the Torah’s emphasis on practical observance over theoretical knowledge.
In this vein, he references the work of 19th century French politician and philosopher, Pierre-Joseph Proudon, regarding Moshe’s intent behind the Torah. According to Proudon, Moshe did not aim to create a theoretical or philosophical doctrine. Rather, his goal was to establish a practical and actionable guide for living, a manual of sorts for the Israelites. This perspective is significant because it positions the Torah as a living document, meant to guide the daily lives and practices of the people of Israel, rather than to serve as a theoretical discourse for the broader nations.
The commentary then considers how the Torah does not explicitly link Rosh Hashana to judgement, but Ḥazal do. He delves into the idea that Rosh Hashanah, like Yom Kippur and Shemini Aṣeret, is fundamentally a day of judgement and forgiveness, illustrated by the unique nature of the sacrifices offered on these days, which differs significantly from those offered on other occasions.
He further draws a parallel between the following verse in Sefer Bemidbar, “and if you go to war in your land against the enemy that oppresses you, then you shall blow with the horn blast; and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God” (10:9) and the observance of Rosh Hashanah, which is described in our verse as “a commemoration with horn blast”. This comparison underscores the significance of the shofar’s sound on Rosh Hashanah – it is not merely a ritual act, but a powerful invocation for remembrance before God, both for the community’s external enemies and for their internal spiritual struggles.
Delving into the Torah’s structure, Rabbi Benamozegh discusses the calendar and its spiritual implications. Now that we have connected Rosh Hashanahh and Yom Kippur, by means of the qorbanot, what are their individual, specific purposes? One of them may indeed be the new year, and Yom Kippur of the yobel (Jubilee) year has a shofar blast, so perhaps the start of the year is on Yom Kippur. However, he questions the logic of the tenth day being the start of the year, instead of the new moon, noting that no other culture or language starts their year in the middle of a month. Thus the ‘new year’ is Rosh Hashana, rather than Yom Kippur. Further, he argues that the gap between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur server as a transitional period between the end of servitude (brought about by the yobel) and the beginning of freedom. These days are seen as a time for spiritual transition, moving from the slavery of physical drives to the freedom of servitude under divine authority. This concept, he notes, is hinted at in the word ‘yobel’, which derives from the root יבל, and connotes movement; in this case, the movement is returning to God. In other words, the Jubilee symbolised a societal reset, where both land and people were released from the bonds of prior transactions and servitude, emphasising restoration, and a return to an original state.
Rabbi Benamozegh then touches upon the dual nature of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. While these days have physical purposes related to national life, they also hold profound spiritual significance. The Written Torah, he explains, focuses on the physical aspects of Rosh Hashana, while the Oral Torah delves into its spiritual and ethical dimensions. On Yom Kippur, both aspects are combined in the written Torah, as it discusses the kappara achieved, which Rabbi Benamozegh views as the return of the soul to its Creator, as well as the return of lands and slaves to their original state.
Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises the Prophets’ use of tangible metaphors to convey spiritual truths, exemplified by the metaphor of the “redeemer” (גואל). In the Torah, a “redeemer” is a relative who buys back land or frees an individual from servitude, embodying familial loyalty and responsibility. This physical concept of redemption is used metaphorically in the Prophets’ writings, where God is often depicted as Israel’s “redeemer”. This metaphorical usage can allow us to grasp the closeness, immediacy, and tangibility of God’s relationship with us, and is thus another example of the physical description serving as a metaphor for the spiritual events.
Rabbi Benamozegh goes on to reference Sefer Melakhim (1:8), which uniquely mentions the seventh month by its original Canaanite, non-Babylonian name: ‘Etanim’. This is equivalent to the Babylonian month of Tishre, and means ‘strong’ or ‘perennial’, in reference to the rivers that still flow with water during Tishre. Ḥazal made a derasha that the ‘strong ones’ of this month refers to the abot, our forefathers. This time, Rabbi Benamozegh states, is thus characterised as an opportunity for individuals to return to their primal, untainted state, which was perceived by the ancients as pure and free from transgression.
Rabbi Benamozegh also links the word ‘Etanim’ to the root אתא, meaning to come in Aramaic, and thus encouraging a return to both ancestral heritage and a deeper connection with God. This is in the same way that ‘yobel’ was connected to the root יבל. He notes that the Targum Yonatan further elucidates this period, referring to this month as the “month of the ancients”, signifying its paramount importance before the Exodus and the establishment of Nissan as the beginning of the Jewish calendar. He quotes the 12th century Rabbi David Qimḥi (Radaq), who notes the unique position of this month in the Jewish calendar. He contrasts it with other cultures where Tishre is the exclusive start of the year, and this power is preserved in its special status in Judaism. However, the use of Nissan as the start of the year is a uniquely Jewish idea.

30.0:
No task shall you do, an everlasting statute for your generations in all your dwelling places.
Rabbi Benamozegh elucidates that the Hebrew word for “generation” (דור) is etymologically linked to the word דירה (‘live’, ‘dwell’, ‘abode’). This connection implies that a ‘generation’ is defined by the span of time during which people live or dwell in the world. The concept of ‘generation’ thus becomes a measure of human existence and presence in the world.
Further exploring this notion, Rabbi Benamozegh references the works of the 12th century Rabbi David Qimḥi (Radaq) and the 13th century Rabbi Shimon ben Ṣemah Duran (Rashbaṣ), who both delve into the root of the word ‘generation’.

39.0:
And you shall take you on the first day the fruit of a majestic tree, fronds of palm trees, and a branch of a leafy tree and willows of the brook, and you shall rejoice before YHWH your God seven days.
Rabbi Benamozegh explores the linguistic and philosophical underpinnings of a key phrase in Jewish law, “fruit of a majestic tree” (פרי עץ הדר). This is commonly understood to refer to the etrog (citron) used during the festival of Sukkot.
Rabbi Benamozegh begins by referencing interpretations from the Talmud Babli, the Talmud Yerushalmi, and Midrash Rabba. In these texts, the interpretation of “hadar” is aligned with the Greek word ‘hudor’, meaning ‘water’. For example, Rabbi Shimon Ben Azzai in the Talmud makes this connection to the Greek language, identifying the fact that the etrog is a fruit that needs constant watering to grow.
Rabbi Benamozegh notes that the 18th century scholar Rabbi Yiṣḥaq ben Yehuda Rapoport is sceptical about the possibility of deriving halakha from a Greek reading of a Hebrew word, as this would usually only be reserved for non-legal elements such as midrash (Biblical exegesis) or aggada (narrative literature). However, Rabbi Benamozegh asserts that Jewish law often incorporates insights from Greek linguistics, among other languages. This assertion is not trivial; it underscores the dynamic and inclusive nature of Jewish legal interpretation, which extends beyond the confines of a single language or culture.
To illustrate this point, Rabbi Benamozegh references the interpretation of a phrase related to capital law, highlighting the Greek linguistic roots that inform Jewish law. The example he uses is based on Vayiqra 20:14 “If a man marries a woman and her mother, it is depravity; both he and they [ואתהן] shall be burned with fire, so that there will be no depravity among you”, where the Greek word ‘hen’ (meaning ‘one’) plays a critical role in its interpretation. He notes that this is expressed in Yalkut Shimoni on the same verse, “The Rabbis taught: ‘They shall be burned with fire, both he and they’ - this refers to him and one of them, as in the Greek language they call one of them ‘hen’.”
Rabbi Benamozegh then shifts to a philosophical discussion, focusing on the efforts of the Greek philosopher Plato. He recounts Plato’s attempt in Cratylus to find a Greek origin for the word for water, believing that the term ‘hudor’ likely originated from another language. Plato supports this by referencing the presence of a similar word to ‘hudor’ among the Phrygian people of Asia.

10.0:
And the son of the Israelite woman invoked the Name, vilifying it. And they brought him to Moshe. And his mother’s name was Shelomith daughter of Dibri of the tribe of Dan.
Rabbi Benamozegh explores the concept of associating a son with his mother’s lineage, as exemplified in our verse.
He notes that the Tanakh frequently names sons after their mothers, as evidenced in various verses such as in Sefer Melakhim II. He also references Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra’s assertion that a mother’s nature is inherited by her son, highlighting this as a possible explanation for why Aharon’s sons, rather than Moshe’s sons, inherited greatness. Rabbi Benamozegh also refers to the Talmudic idea that sons often resemble their mother’s brothers due to the prenatal environment. However, he challenges the notion that this is the reason why Moshe’s sons were not chosen to lead the people after him. He points out that leadership in Jewish society is meritocratic, rather than an inherited position, and thus Moshe’s sons were not chosen for that reason, rather than a negative influence from their mother’s side.
Finally, Rabbi Benamozegh contrasts Israelite matrilineal customs with those of other ancient cultures. He points out that matronymics (naming children after their mothers) was also practised by the ancient Etruscans and Greeks, particularly in their burial traditions. This contrasts sharply with Egyptian customs, where maternal lineage was undervalued. He suggests that this difference is one of the ways in which the God of Israel set His people apart from Egyptian ideas and practices.

14.0:
And to the Israelites you shall speak, saying ‘Should any man vilify his God, he shall bear his offense.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into a comprehensive analysis of the prohibition against vilifying/cursing gods.
At the outset, Rabbi Benamozegh references interpretations from a wide range of sources, including the 1st century Jewish historian Josephus, the 1st century BCE Jewish scholar Philo, and the Essenes of the Second Temple era. (Tangentially, he regards the Essenes as forerunners to the Kabbalists). These sources, despite their varied backgrounds, unanimously interpret our verse as prohibiting blasphemy not only against God, but against the gods of other nations. This consensus underscores a universal moral directive against disrespecting any deity, reflecting a deep-seated reverence for the divine, regardless of religious boundaries.
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses the Zohar, which appeared in late 13th century Ashkenaz. The Zohar similarly prohibits cursing foreign deities, echoing the sentiment of the previously mentioned sources. This interpretation is grounded in the belief that all gods exist by divine permission to govern different nations. Based on this, he criticises those who accused Josephus and Philo of fabricating this interpretation of the verse, in order to appease their respective Roman and Greek compatriots. The Zohar has no need to appease any other nation, and yet echoes their statements wholeheartedly.
Reflecting on the origins of the Zohar’s teachings, Rabbi Benamozegh ponders whether the Zohar’s author might have been influenced by earlier Jewish scholars such as Josephus and Philo. He suggests that if the Zohar’s author arrived at these interpretations independently, they were likely formulated during an era when such ideas were already well-established and recognised among the scholarly Jewish community. This period, he infers, would align with the time of the early Tannaim.
Rabbi Benamozegh then explores Kabbalistic beliefs such as the notion that every idol mentioned in holy texts contains an element of holiness. This Kabbalistic perspective leads to a prohibition against cursing idols or Satan, as it would amount to cursing something that possesses a divine spark. This belief highlights the nuanced understanding of divinity in Kabbalistic thought, where even entities traditionally viewed as negative are seen as part of a larger divine plan. Notably, Rabbi Benamozegh stresses that Philo’s primary concern was to prevent other nations from cursing the God of Israel. This concern reflects a protective stance towards one’s own deity while also respecting others.
Rabbi Benamozegh then connects this ancient prohibition to texts such as the 2nd century Ben Sira (“when the ungodly curses Satan, he curses his own soul”) and the 1st century work, Second Epistle of Peter, to illustrate the ancient roots of this belief. In the second chapter, the author castigates those human beings who slander and blaspheme the celestial beings, even though angels – who sit above those celestial beings – do not blaspheme them, even as they bring judgement upon them. Rabbi Benamozegh observes that this aligns with the perspective of the Zohar, that it is inappropriate to curse those ministering beings whom some worship as idols; the Zohar calls these beings ‘shiltonin de’alema’. This is explained in more detail in the Epistle of Jude, where the author rebukes those individuals, and points out that the archangel Michael, when arguing with Satan over Moshe’s body, said to Satan merely, “May the Lord rebuke you!”. Taking these two sources together, Rabbi Benamozegh concludes that the author of 2 Peter was criticising those human beings who curse Satan, instead taking the stance that it was forbidden to do so, in accordance with Philo, Josephus, the Essenes and the Kabbalists. Rabbi Benamozegh views this as a further indication that Christianity emerged from the Essenes, when they corrupted Kabbalistic teachings by bringing them into mundane spheres.
Rabbi Benamozegh moves on to the Talmudic tractate Qiddushin, which reflects similar sentiments. He recounts the story in it of Pelemo who was accustomed to say every day, “arrows in the eyes of Satan”. One day, Satan revealed himself to him and asked, “Why do you say this?” Pelemo replied asking what he could say instead, and Satan said, “May the Merciful one rebuke Satan,” clearly echoing the language of the Epistle of Jude. Another moral derived from this aggada, notes Rabbi Benamozegh, aligns with the Kabbalistic view of not standing in the way of the agents of judgement when they perform their mission. The Kabbalists refer to this as ‘ḥasima’, or ‘blocking’, which is the metaphysical idea of restricting divine flow or energy.
Extending this principle, Rabbi Benamozegh discusses broader applications in Jewish practice, such as the prohibition against giving charity at night. He refers to the aggada that details how Rabbi Eleazar was distributing charity at night and encountered the chief spirit of the dead, who challenged his doing so on the basis that night is the time allocated to spirits, and not to human beings; Rabbi Eleazar’s distribution of charity was interfering with the non-human agents carrying out God’s will during the night. He argues that these practices, such as not giving charity at night, whilst ostensibly new, are rooted in deep theological beliefs, tracing back to ancient traditions.
14.1: Lastly, Rabbi Benamozegh references the Qur’an, suggesting that Muhammad’s teachings against cursing idols were influenced by Jewish traditions. This further reinforces his argument that this interpretation of the pasuq was widespread at the time of the Mishna, and carried by Jews to Arab lands.

1.0:
Speak to the Israelites, and you shall say to them: ‘When you come into the land that I am about to give you, the land shall keep a sabbath to YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh presents a deep and insightful analysis that intertwines the concept of Sabbatical years with the festivals.
The Sabbatical year (‘shemita’) is a period every seventh year when the land of Israel is left fallow and agricultural activities are halted.
He begins by presenting us with an observation made by Shadal about Israelite timekeeping: just as the Jubilee year (‘yobel’) occurs every fifty years, following seven cycles of seven Sabbatical years, similarly, the Israelite festivals are scheduled in a pattern that mirrors this. Shadal notes that the total number of Sabbaths in a year is always at least forty-nine, but never reaches fifty-six. This means that the number of Sabbaths each year is never divisible by a whole number greater or smaller than seven. Correspondingly, there are seven significant days in the Jewish liturgical calendar that are considered “holy convocations”. These are the first and seventh days of Passover, one day of Shabuot, one of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, the first day of Sukkot, and Shemini Aṣeret. Each of these days has a special significance, cumulatively adding up to seven days, mirroring the Sabbatical cycle. The shemita year falls once every seven years, and the yobel falls once every seven shemita years. Similarly, the Sabbath falls once every seven days, and there are seven festivals each year, which works out to one festival per seven Sabbaths each year.
Rabbi Benamozegh concludes by reflecting on the delight and profundity of these observations, inviting the reader to appreciate the intricate and interconnected nature of the Torah’s teachings. He emphasises that while this relationship may not be immediately apparent or explicitly written in the Torah, it underscores a deeper, underlying unity within the Torah’s laws.

9.0:
And you shall hallow the fiftieth year and call a release in the land to all its inhabitants. A jubilee it shall be for you, and you shall go back each man to his holding and each man to his clan, you shall go back.
Rabbi Benamozegh provides a multi-layered interpretation of the Jubilee year (יובל). His analysis explores the Jubilee year’s theological, philosophical, and chronological aspects, engaging with both Jewish and non-Jewish scholarly perspectives.
The first part of his commentary on our verse delves into the Kabbalistic interpretation of the Jubilee year. He notes that Kabbalists view the Jubilee as symbolising the return of reality to its source - God. They link the Kabbalistic attribute of understanding (‘binah’) with ‘repentance’ (‘teshuba’) and Jubilee (‘yobel’), which both connote the idea of ‘returning’. By associating ‘binah’ with the Jubilee, Kabbalists emphasise the idea of returning or reverting to a purer, more Divine state. This interpretation aligns with the broader Kabbalistic theme of restoring balance and harmony to the universe through human actions and Divine grace.
Rabbi Benamozegh then addresses how the concept of Jubilee is deeply ingrained in the commandments and has influenced external perceptions. He notes that some researchers and individuals mistakenly believed that the Jubilee was established based on the idea that the world would end every fifty years. This misinterpretation, he explains, is a result of confusing the metaphor with the thing it symbolises. In other words, the symbolic meaning of the Jubilee — a time of restoration and renewal — was misread as a literal end of the world. This highlights the potential for misinterpretation when symbolic religious concepts are taken out of their theological and cultural context.
Moving on, Rabbi Benamozegh addresses a chronological and interpretative error made by some scholars of the nations, including the 16th century philosophers Scaliger and Pétau, who posited that the Jubilee year was the forty-ninth year. He refutes this by citing the explicit text in our verse, “and you shall hallow the fiftieth year.” He notes that other earlier scholars like Josephus, Philo, Eusebius, and Jerome correctly acknowledged the Jubilee as the fiftieth year.
Lastly, Rabbi Benamozegh brings in a rabbinic perspective from the Talmud, where there is a debate in Nedarim regarding whether the fiftieth-year counts in the cycle of seven (the Sabbatical cycle). The dispute between Rabbi Yehudah, who holds that it does count, and the Sages, who hold that it does not, possibly led to the confusion among the aforementioned earlier scholars.

22.0:
And the land shall not be sold irreversibly, for Mine is the land, for you are sojourning settlers with Me.
Rabbi Benamozegh examines the interpretations of the phrase “for Mine is the land” as understood by Rashi and the 13th century scholar, Naḥmanides. Although Rabbi Naftali Wessely distinguished between these two opinions, in Rabbi Benamozegh’s opinion both commentators agree that the verse highlights God’s sovereignty over the land, suggesting that it should not be sold in perpetuity.
Further, Rabbi Benamozegh addresses Rabbi Wessely’s interpretation that the verse essentially conveys the idea: ‘I am the Lord of the land, and it is within My power to command what I desire.’ However, Rabbi Benamozegh critiques this view, observing that it diverges from the interpretations of both Rashi and Naḥmanides. He argues that adopting this proposed rationale behind the commandment could potentially apply to any land-related commandment, and does not explain why this particular commandment was given.

24.0:
If one of your kin is in straits and has to sell part of a holding, the nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what that relative has sold.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the historical and philosophical context surrounding the sale of ancestral property.
He begins by highlighting the inherent difficulty faced by an Israelite in selling his ancestral heritage, a concept deeply rooted in the Torah and the chronicles of Jewish history. This difficulty is not merely a matter of legality but is steeped in a profound sense of cultural and spiritual responsibility towards one’s heritage.
Rabbi Benamozegh then draws parallels with the wisdom of ancient philosophers, particularly those who journeyed to Egypt and learned from its priests. These philosophers, he notes, gained deep insights into the governance and ethical management of society. A notable reference to Plato is made, who, in Book V of Laws, emphasised the sanctity of ancestral land. Plato articulately warned against taking lightly one’s inherited land. He advises against engaging in its trade or sale, underscoring that such actions would not only displease God, who decreed the division of the land, but also go against the intentions of the legislator.
Furthermore, Rabbi Benamozegh references the land of Lacedaemon in ancient Greece, where the sale of ancestral property was explicitly prohibited. This example serves to illustrate the widespread recognition, across different cultures and societies, of the importance of preserving ancestral heritage.
He also touches upon the legal perspectives expressed by the formative rabbinic scholars of Ashkenazi Jewry, the Tosafot, active during the 12th-14th centuries. The Talmud records a dispute between Rab Yehuda quoting Shemuel and Rab, regarding whether everything stated in the Perashat Hamelekh (a list found in I Shemuel 8:11-17) is permitted for a king to do. Included in this list is that a king may take land as he sees fit. Rabbi Benamozegh then refers to the Tosafot, who argued that the field of Naboth, as described in Sefer Melakhim I, was ancestral property, and therefore, even according to Rab Yehuda (who allows for a king to seize property as he sees fit), Naboth was under no obligation to relinquish it to King Ahab. Consequently, Ahab’s murder of Naboth was unjustified.

39.0:
Like a paid worker, like a resident slave he shall be under you, till the jubilee year he shall work under you, and he shall be released from you
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the complexities of this verse, particularly in the context of the Jubilee year and the status of Canaanite slaves (referred to here as a “toshab”, ‘resident’) and employed workers (referred to here as a “sakhir”, ‘hireling’)
He begins by highlighting an apparent contradiction in different verses of Vayiqra. On one hand, our verse compares the release of an Israelite slave – which takes place at yobel – to the release of a Canaanite slave, suggesting that a Canaanite slave, is to be released in the Jubilee year. However, this interpretation becomes problematic when considering the subsequent verses, which imply that Canaanite slaves never go free, and instead are ‘inherited’ when the master dies.
Rabbi Benamozegh notes that this contradiction seems to have been overlooked by many, with the exception of himself and the 13th century Rabbi Levi ben Gershon (Ralbag). Ralbag tries to resolve this contradiction by suggesting that the verse means that the Israelite slave, in this context, has elements which are similar to a paid worker (sakhir), and elements which are similar to a Canaanite slave (toshab). However, Rabbi Benamozegh finds Ralbag’s explanation unsatisfactory as it does not align with the straightforward meaning of the verse.
Adding to the complexity, Rabbi Benamozegh references Rabbi Naftali Wessely, who also tried to resolve this contradiction by suggesting two separate definitions of the word ‘toshab’, one for our verse (which suggests that he goes free at yobel) and one for the later verse (which suggests that he does not). However, Rabbi Benamozegh believes that Rabbi Wessely’s efforts were ultimately unsuccessful too. This leaves Rabbi Benamozegh in a state of uncertainty about how to reconcile these conflicting interpretations. He expresses his ongoing contemplation and the need for further thought to understand the explanation behind the verses.

46.0:
And should the hand of a sojourning settler with you attain means when your brother comes to ruin under you and is sold to a sojourning settler under you, or to a root of a sojourner’s clan
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the interpretation of the term “root” (עקר) as it appears in this verse. He notes that according to Ḥazal, the “root” refers to idolatry, and it refers to a slave who was sold to assist in serving idolatry.
Rabbi Benamozegh references Rabbi Naftali Wessely, who proposes that idolatry is termed “root” because it is something that must be completely uprooted and eradicated. However, Rabbi Benamozegh finds this explanation somewhat tenuous and instead offers his own understanding.
He suggests that “root” is metaphorically used in the same way ‘source’ might be, specifically in the context of idol worship. This metaphorical usage aligns with how the Sages often personify God as ‘The Root’ (iqar), implying that He is the fundamental source of all existence. This interpretation is further supported by the phrase “to a root of a sojourner’s clan” in our verse, as Rabbi Benamozegh notes that families among the non-Jewish nations were often identified by their gods (such as Lares and Penates, who were groups of deities dedicated to protecting the family and the Roman state; in essence, household gods).
Additionally, he observes that these families traced their lineage and origins through their ancestors and forefathers, leading back to their idols. Therefore, in this context, idolatry is aptly referred to as ‘the root of a sojourner’s family,’ indicating its deep-seated and foundational role in the identity and heritage of these families. This understanding provides a more nuanced interpretation of the term “root” in our verse, linking it to the profound and intrinsic connection between idolatry and the familial and cultural identities of the nations.

52.0:
No one shall hold crushing sway over him before your eyes
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the ethical and moral dimensions of this injunction.
He references an interpretation of the Sifra that addresses a potential misunderstanding. One might incorrectly assume that it is permissible to intrude into the private quarters of one’s slave, to see that he is acting correctly. The Sifra clarifies that “before your eyes” (לעיניך) restricts the jurisdiction of the master to what is directly observable by him, without intrusion into the slave’s private environment.
Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises the timeless relevance of this teaching, arguing that it was ahead of its time in advocating for the respect of privacy and personal boundaries. He suggests that in modern times, when the inclination to probe into others’ affairs has perhaps grown, this ancient wisdom remains profoundly pertinent. He highlights the importance of this prohibition with regards to the legislative power searching through people’s homes in order to know what takes place in them. He points out that the directive holds regardless of the social or religious status of the individuals involved, even in a case where, for example, an Israelite slave is owned by a Gentile, and the Israelites are in power. There is still no right for the Israelite government to invade the privacy of the Gentile to discover what takes place in his private domain.
Rabbi Benamozegh extends this discussion by linking it to another similar commandment found in Debarim 24:10-11: “Should you make a loan of anything to your fellow man, you shall not come into his house to take his pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you made the loan shall bring out the pledge to you outside.” He draws a parallel between these restrictions, noting that both advocate for a respectful distance and a boundary in interactions, especially in situations with uneven power dynamics, where those in power are likely to resort to a more invasive approach, such as taking collateral for a loan.

0.0:
You shall make you no idols nor set up a sculptured image or a sacred pillar for yourselves, and you shall not put a figured stone in your land to bow over it, for I am YHWH your God.
Rabbi Benamozegh offers a critical analysis of the concept of the “figured stone” (אבן משכית) and engages in a scholarly debate with the interpretations of the 13th century Naḥmanides on this verse.
Rabbi Benamozegh questions Naḥmanides’ notion that the “figured stone” refers to a stone with Egyptian hieroglyphs, used in priestly rituals. He challenges this view by pointing out the inconsistency in the idea of the Israelites being commanded to “bow” or prostrate themselves upon such a stone, as this was not even a custom in Egyptian worship. He argues that if the intention were to worship towards the stone, the text would have explicitly stated ‘to prostrate towards it,’ rather than ‘to prostrate upon it.’
Rabbi Benamozegh then presents his own interpretation, likening the “figured stone” to a pillar, drawing a parallel with the Biblical episode where Ya’aqob erects a stone as a pillar to mark the place where God had spoken to him via his dream (Bereshit 35:14). Rabbi Benamozegh suggests that pillars such as these could be referred to by the term “figured stone” because they were set in covers of precious metals, similar to the imagery described in Proverbs 25:11 of “golden apples in silver filigrees” (תפוחי זהב במשכיות כסף). He also makes a reference to the stone of the Ka’aba in Mecca, a key feature of the Islamic tradition, which is similarly covered in such a manner.
Rabbi Benamozegh explains that the reason the verse prohibited prostration upon these stones is because such stones were positioned lower than the worshipper, facilitating a physical act of prostration and kissing, as an expression of reverence and worship.
Finally, he points out that the stones described in this verse are the same as those referenced in the Biblical directive to dispel idolatry, as seen in Bemidbar 33:52, where the Israelites are commanded to dispossess the land’s inhabitants and destroy all their “figured stones” and their “sculptured images”.

20.0:
And if you come in with happenstance against Me and do not want to heed Me, I will go on with blows against you sevenfold for your offenses.
Rabbi Benamozegh begins by referencing a commentary from Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra that addresses the term קרי, which connotes ‘randomness’, ‘chance’, or ‘happenstance’.
According to Ibn Ezra’s second interpretation, the meaning of this term can be understood by referring to the narrative involving the Philistines in Sefer Shemuel (I 6:9). That verse conveys the idea that the harm inflicted upon the Philistines was not a result of God’s direct intervention but rather described as a ‘random’ event or ‘chance’ that occurred to them. Rabbi Benamozegh agrees with this interpretation, viewing it as a caution against failing to acknowledge God’s role in worldly events. He then cites Rabbi Naftali Wessely’s difficulty with this understanding, as how could God say that He will also walk ‘happenstance’ with the Israelites? Surely everything that occurs is due to God’s decree. Rabbi Benamozegh refutes his argument in the following manner.
Rabbi Benamozegh agrees with the position of Ibn Ezra, interpreting the verse as expressing a profound theological concept: when humans attribute every life experience merely to chance, disregarding Divine providence, there is a corresponding Divine response. This Divine response is itself the ‘leaving of things to chance’ on God’s part, acting as though there were no Israelites, in imitation of the behaviour of the Israelites acting as if there were no God.
To underscore this interpretation, Rabbi Benamozegh references Torah verses such as when the people will say, “Because there is no God in our midst” (Debarim 31:17-18), where God speaks of hiding His face in response to disobedience. He contrasts this with Debarim 11:12, “the eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it,” reflecting the idea that God’s vigilant care and guidance are contingent on the acknowledgment of His presence and role in human life.
Rabbi Benamozegh also delves into the linguistic nuances of a later verse in Vayiqra (26:24), “and I will come in happenstance against you.” He points out that this wording appears “strained”, suggesting this is “the way of the scribes” to draw a parallel between seemingly disparate concepts. This linguistic style is used to juxtapose the idea of God walking with people in a state of happenstance, or apparent randomness (as opposed to the more direct expressions of God leaving or hiding His face), with the Israelites doing the same. This creates a textual symmetry, adhering to the principle of “measure for measure” (מדה כנגד מדה). This principle, a recurring theme in Rabbinic theology, indicates that God’s responses are proportionate and directly related to human actions, emphasising a reciprocal relationship between Divine response and human behaviour.

44.0:
And I will remember for them the Covenant of the first ones whom I brought out from the land of Egypt before the eyes of the nations to be God for them, I am YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh interprets this verse as a reference to the special Covenant established with the ancestors who emerged from the land of Egypt.
These ancestors, in the context of their descendants, are specifically those from the generation of Moshe. This interpretation is further supported by Yirmiyahu 2:2, “I recall the goodness of your youth, your love as a bride”, which poetically recalls the early, formative period of the Israelites’ relationship with God during and after their Exodus from Egypt.
Rabbi Benamozegh emphasises that our verse underscores the enduring nature of the Covenant between God and the Israelites, passed down through generations. The Covenant is not merely a historical agreement but a living bond that continues to resonate with the descendants of those who initially received it. This continuous connection, as Rabbi Benamozegh suggests, is pivotal in understanding Judaism’s emphasis on the collective memory and the spiritual legacy of their ancestors.

27.0:
But anything proscribed, that a man may proscribe for YHWH, of anything he has, whether of humans or animals or of the field of his holding, shall not be sold and shall not be redeemed. Anything proscribed is holy of holies to YHWH.
Rabbi Benamozegh delves into the interpretation of “ḥerem” (חרם), a key term in Jewish thought. His exploration goes beyond the confines of Jewish tradition to include a broader context of ancient legal systems and societal norms, shedding light on the multifaceted nature of this word and its implications.
This term typically connotes ‘dedicated’ or ‘proscribed’. These connotations are based on the interpretation of this word in the Talmud, which Rabbi Benamozegh explores in his commentary. He notes that Ḥazal use this word in this verse to support the idea that individuals facing execution are ‘dedicated’, and therefore cannot be ‘redeemed’ - i.e., they cannot consecrate their value to the temple (Arakhin 6b).
Rabbi Benamozegh shows that this term was used to denote individuals condemned to death in ancient legal context too. He asserts that the ancients called anyone condemned to death as being ‘ḥerem’ to the Lord, even in human legal terms. Rabbi Benamozegh sources this from Giambattista Vico, who wrote that the Twelve Tables of Rome (an ancient Roman legal code) mandated that anyone who violated a Tribune of the Plebs (an important official in Ancient Rome) was ‘consecrated to Jove’, a rebellious son was ‘consecrated to the gods of the fathers’, and anyone who burnt the produce of another was ‘consecrated to Ceres’ and executed by burning.
Rabbi Benamozegh further enhances this discussion by linking ‘ḥerem’ to the divine authority behind human justice. He emphasises that in ancient thought, the judgement and punishment by human judges were seen as extensions of divine authority, granted by that divine authority. This theological perspective lays the foundation for understanding human justice as intrinsically tied to divine will, providing a rationale for ancient legal practices.
The commentary then takes a critical turn as Rabbi Benamozegh addresses and refutes two alternative interpretations of this verse.
The first interpretation that Rabbi Benamozegh confronts is the idea that anyone who makes a ‘ḥerem’ (i.e. ‘proscribing’ or ‘dedicating’) from among people shall not be redeemed but shall die. This interpretation is partly grounded in the narrative of Yiftaḥ’s daughter, in Sefer Shofetim 11:30-40. In this story, Yiftaḥ vows to offer the first thing that comes out of his house to greet him as a burnt offering to God, should he return victorious from battle. Tragically, his daughter is the first to greet him, leading to interpretations that she was sacrificed or devoted to a perpetual service to God, depending on different readings. The text of this narrative does not explicitly use the term ‘ḥerem’, but the term is often brought into the discussion as it fits in the broader concept of ‘dedicating’ or ‘devoting’ something to God. However, Rabbi Benamozegh refutes this interpretation of ‘ḥerem’ as exclusively or primarily signifying a death sentence. He seems to argue that such a reading is overly narrow and does not capture the broader, more nuanced meanings and applications of the word within Jewish law and tradition.
The second interpretation that Rabbi Benamozegh challenges views ‘ḥerem’ as a decree or decision that could be proclaimed by public leaders or even the general populace, as a temporary emergency measure (hora’at sha’a), even to the extent of putting people to death. Rabbi Benamozegh argues that this overextends the authority granted in the Torah. In reality, he does not see this special dispensation given by Ḥazal to a court as explicitly sourced in the Written Torah.
Rejecting both alternative explanations, Rabbi Benamozegh circles back to the Jewish legal tradition, highlighting that individuals executed by the Sanhedrin are considered ‘ḥerem’ (‘devoted’ or ‘proscribed’) to God, in accordance with the terminology of other ancient traditions. This perspective aligns with the understanding that ultimate judgment and law are in the hands of God, as expressed in Yeshayahu 33:22, “God shall be our Judge, God shall be our Lawgiver.”
He states that this viewpoint is further elucidated by Rashi’s interpretation of Ḥazal’s statements in Arakhin 6b, explored above. Rashi confirms that if someone attempts to redeem an individual who is condemned to death, the redemption is essentially null and void. This interpretation underscores the idea that once a person is sentenced to death, they are beyond the realm of ordinary human transactions or interventions, such as ransom or monetary redemption. They are, in essence, ‘ḥerem’ or ‘dedicated’ to God, meaning they fall under Divine jurisdiction and human actions such as making vows on their value become irrelevant. This principle serves as a warning and a reminder of the gravity of capital cases and the limitations of human intervention in matters that are ultimately governed by divine law and judgment.
Rabbi Benamozegh proceeds to contrast the Jewish concept of ‘ḥerem’ with ancient views on sacrifice and deities. He points out how Latin terms like ‘sacer’ (sacred) were used in the word ‘execrabilis’, connoting ‘consecrated to death by judgement’. However, further linguistic analysis reveals the stark differences between Israelite and pagan sacrificial practices, particularly the abhorrent practice of human sacrifice prevalent in other cultures. The Latin term ‘hostia’ can refer to both an intended sacrifice, as well as a victim, which Rabbi Benamozegh links to the phrase ‘hostis victus’, meaning ‘the defeated enemy’, which he views as an indication that once defeated, enemies were sacrificed.
Rabbi Benamozegh concludes his commentary by arguing that this linguistic distinction not only showcases the moral superiority of Hebrew culture but also refutes the claim that Hebrew is part of the Canaanite languages. The absence of terms related to human sacrifice in Hebrew, as opposed to their clear presence in other languages, serves as evidence of its unique and elevated nature.
